META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 1.3 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.content:
• Kingdom Plantae (general characteristics of organisms in Divisions Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta; include sub-divisions and classes of Spermatophyta)
• Kingdom Animalia (general characteristics of organisms in Chordata and Arthropoda up to class level; include economic importance of arthropods)
• Dichotomous keys (principles of construction, identification of organisms, and practical applications)
• Viruses (general characteristics, conditions for their growth, and economic importance)
• Projects: preparing herbarium specimens and mounting animal specimens or their images using locally available materials
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner speaks clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of various specimens (Lessons 1–8), working in groups to agree on classification criteria, build keys and present findings.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners decide which characteristics are useful for classification, solve identification problems and justify classification decisions (Lessons 1, 4, 6 and 8).
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner experiments with varied ideas while preparing a herbarium of plant specimens, and designs classification charts, dichotomous keys and biodiversity guides (Lessons 3, 4 and 8).
UNIT.values:
• Respect: The learner is considerate of others' opinions while brainstorming on the characteristics of viruses and their economic importance, and listens to alternative classification ideas.
• Responsibility: The learner cares for the environment while collecting specimens of monocot and dicot plants, and handles specimens and learning resources carefully.
• Excellence: Learners strive for accuracy when identifying and classifying organisms.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions: Learners generate questions for the Driving Question Board about how organisms are grouped and why viruses matter.
• Developing and using models: Learners build and revise classification charts and dichotomous keys across the unit.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: Learners compare observed features of plants and animals in tables to find patterns.
• Constructing explanations: Learners use evidence from specimens to justify why an organism belongs in a division, phylum or class.
• Engaging in argument from evidence: Learners defend classification decisions to peers and revise them when given new evidence.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: Learners use textbooks, readings and diagrams to learn about viruses and present group keys.
UNIT.pcis:
• Environmental Conservation: The learner conserves biodiversity by responsibly collecting organisms for the preparation of herbarium specimens.
• Animal Welfare: The learner handles animals with care while observing and grouping them into Phylum Chordata and Arthropoda using distinguishing characteristics.
• Health and disease awareness: Learners relate viruses to human, animal and plant diseases and their prevention.
• Environmental sustainability and responsible use of biological resources: Learners appreciate why biodiversity should be documented and used wisely.
UNIT.careers:
• Biology teacher: teaches classification and guides learners in identifying organisms.
• Botanist: classifies plants into divisions and prepares herbarium collections, for example at the National Museums of Kenya.
• Zoologist: groups animals into phyla and classes.
• Ecologist: uses classification to study biodiversity in habitats such as the Rift Valley and Lake Victoria.
• Taxonomist: names, describes and organises organisms using keys.
• Agricultural scientist: identifies crop plants, pests and plant viruses affecting maize and beans.
• Veterinary professional: identifies animals and viral diseases of livestock.
• Wildlife officer: identifies species in parks and reserves such as Maasai Mara.
• Environmental scientist: monitors biodiversity and sustainability.
• Laboratory technologist: handles specimens and identifies disease-causing agents such as viruses.
• Research scientist: studies viruses and biodiversity, including in biotechnology.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses familiar organisms from the school and local environment (maize, beans, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, earthworm, chicken, goat) to build understanding of how plants, animals and viruses are classified. Learners first sort organisms using their own criteria, then compare these with scientific classification of Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia, practise using and constructing dichotomous keys, and explore viruses. Local specimens, pictures and textbooks are used so activities do not depend on internet access, and learners may discuss in Kiswahili or mother tongue before recording scientific terms in English.
UNIT.phenomenon: The teacher displays or takes learners outside to observe a collection of organisms found around the school and local environment: a maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat. All are living things, yet they differ greatly in structure, size, body covering, way of moving and reproduction. Learners are asked: "If all these organisms are living things, how can scientists organise them into groups so that any person anywhere can identify and study them?" It is puzzling because learners' own groupings (for example by size, colour, habitat or usefulness as food) differ from group to group, and no single grouping works for everyone. This shows the need for a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Two groups of learners sort the same set of organisms differently (by habitat versus by body structure), and neither can easily tell another group how to identify an unknown specimen.
• A fern and a moss grow side by side on a damp wall or shaded stream bank, yet one has true roots, vascular tissue and fronds while the other is small and lacks these structures.
• Maize and bean plants grow together in a Kenyan farm intercrop, but their leaves, roots and seeds differ (monocot versus dicot).
• A farmer in Kisumu or Nairobi notices that maize leaves show streaking caused by a virus, while a mosquito and a housefly carry different diseases: viruses are not like other organisms and cannot be treated as the rest.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How are plants and animals classified?
2. How are viruses important in nature?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Why classify organisms? Organisms can be grouped using similarities and differences, but scientists require a standard system of classification. Learners observe local organisms/pictures, independently classify them, compare groupings, discuss differences and begin the DQB. Resources: local specimens, organism pictures, manila paper, markers, textbooks, video, exit ticket. Leads to: How do scientists decide which characteristics should be used for classification?
Lesson 2: Kingdom Plantae — Bryophyta. Bryophytes have distinctive characteristics that separate them from other plant groups. Learners observe moss or pictures/specimens, examine structures, record similarities and differences, and make a labelled drawing. Resources: moss specimens/pictures, hand lenses, charts, textbooks, video. Leads to: What makes other plants different from bryophytes?
Lesson 3: Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta. Pteridophytes and spermatophytes have features that distinguish them from bryophytes and from each other. Learners examine ferns, maize, beans or other available plants, compare roots, stems, leaves and reproductive structures, and construct a comparison table. Resources: ferns, maize/bean plants, specimens/pictures, charts, videos. Leads to: How can we classify plants systematically when we encounter an unknown plant?
Lesson 4: Using dichotomous keys. A dichotomous key uses pairs of contrasting characteristics to identify organisms. Learners study a sample key, use it to identify local plants, and create a simple key for collected plant specimens. Resources: plant specimens, prepared keys, worksheets, rulers, video. Leads to: Can the same method be used to identify animals?
Lesson 5: Kingdom Animalia — major phyla. Animals can be classified into major phyla according to characteristic body features. Learners observe pictures/specimens of animals, identify body characteristics, group organisms and justify placement in different phyla. Resources: animal specimens/pictures, charts, textbooks, video. Leads to: How are animals within the same phylum further classified?
Lesson 6: Classes of Kingdom Animalia. Animal phyla can be divided further into classes using more specific characteristics. Learners examine examples of animals, complete classification tables, compare body covering, limbs, respiration and reproduction, and defend classifications. Resources: animal pictures/specimens, charts, classification cards, video. Leads to: How can we identify an unknown animal accurately?
Lesson 7: Dichotomous keys for animals and viruses. Dichotomous keys can identify organisms using observable contrasting features; viruses have distinctive characteristics and importance. Learners construct and use an animal dichotomous key, discuss virus characteristics and their effects, and revise initial ideas. Resources: animal cards, prepared keys, virus diagrams, textbook/readings, video. Leads to: How can our classification system help us explain biodiversity and the importance of viruses?
Lesson 8: Synthesis and explanation. Classification provides an organised system for identifying, studying and communicating about biodiversity. Learners revisit the DQB, complete a final classification challenge, present group models/keys and use evidence to answer the driving question. Resources: organism cards/specimens, charts, learners' notes, rubric, video. Leads to: How can classification knowledge be applied outside the classroom?

LESSONS.title: Why classify organisms?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: classification, taxonomy, similarities, differences, observable characteristics, standard system, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Animalia, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the unit by confronting learners with a collection of local organisms that they must group themselves. Learners discover that different groups use different criteria, and that a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics is needed so anyone can identify and study organisms.
slo.knowledge: Organisms can be grouped using similarities and differences. Groupings based on size, colour, habitat or usefulness vary from person to person. Scientists therefore need a standard system of classification based on shared, observable characteristics. This links to KICD outcome (c): classify organisms into phyla and classes of Kingdom Animalia and Kingdom Plantae, and prepares for outcomes (a) and (b) on Divisions of Kingdom Plantae.
slo.skills: Observing and recording structural features of organisms; classifying using self-chosen criteria; communicating reasoning (SEP: Constructing Explanations); comparing and critiquing groupings (SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence); asking questions (SEP: Asking Questions); developing an initial model (SEP: Developing and Using Models). Core competency: Communication and Collaboration - the learner speaks clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of various specimens.
slo.attitudes: Respect: the learner is considerate of others' opinions when groupings differ. Responsibility: the learner cares for the environment while collecting and handling specimens. Appreciation of the diversity of plants and animals in nature (KICD outcome e). PCIs: Environmental Conservation - collect only common, safe organisms responsibly; Animal Welfare - handle animals with care and return them to where they were found.
slo.keyInquiry: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately? (KICD inquiry: How are plants and animals classified?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 creates the need for the unit. Learners see that all the organisms are living things, yet their own groupings conflict. This raises the question for Lesson 2: How do scientists decide which characteristics should be used for classification? The initial model and the DQB are revisited in Lessons 4 and 8.
slo.safetyNotes: Do NOT collect unknown, venomous or dangerous organisms. Do not touch wild mushrooms with bare hands, and never taste any specimen. The teacher should handle the mushroom, lizard and mosquito (use a pictured or dead specimen). Wash hands after handling soil, earthworms, snails or plants. Handle live animals (earthworm, snail, lizard) gently and return them to their habitat after the lesson. Use photographs for any organism that is unavailable or unsafe. Keep learners supervised outdoors and away from roads, water edges and thorny areas.

LESSONS.overview: Learners walk around the school compound (or view a table display) to observe a maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat (using photographs where specimens are unavailable). They first predict how scientists would group them, then observe closely and independently sort the organisms using their own criteria. Groups put their groupings on manila paper and do a gallery walk to compare. They notice that groupings by size, colour, habitat or food value differ, and that no single grouping works for everyone. Through Think-Pair-Share, learners explain why a standard system is needed. The class opens the Driving Question Board (DQB) with their questions and draws an initial model of how organisms could be grouped. An exit ticket checks understanding and leads to Lesson 2: How do scientists decide which characteristics should be used for classification?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners stand around the display of organisms or photographs: maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat. The teacher asks: 'If all these organisms are living things, how can scientists organise them into groups so that any person anywhere - in Kisumu, Mombasa or Nairobi - can identify and study them?' Individually, learners write a prediction in their notebooks: (1) how many groups they think are needed, (2) what they would use to decide the groups, and (3) whether their groups would match their neighbour's. They discuss ideas first in Kiswahili or mother tongue if helpful, but record key words in English (e.g., 'plant', 'animal', 'group'). They then Think-Pair-Share their predictions with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Before class, gather safe, common local specimens or pictures and arrange them on desks or a table with number tags 1-13. Say: 'All of these are living things. Look carefully for 2 minutes without talking. What do you notice that is the same? What is different?' Pose the phenomenon question aloud and write it on the board. Give 1 minute silent writing time, then say: 'Turn to your partner and share your prediction.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking 'What would you use to make your groups?' before taking any answers. Cold-call 4 learners (different parts of the room) to share a partner's idea, not their own: 'Tell us what your partner predicted.' Record criteria on the board without judging them as right or wrong (e.g., size, colour, habitat, food value). Do NOT give the term 'taxonomy' yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) - Predict step. Recording predictions before evidence makes learners' prior ideas visible and gives them something to compare with later evidence, which promotes conceptual change. Think-Pair-Share lets every learner voice an idea before whole-class discussion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks as you move around: Do 80% of learners write a prediction that includes at least one criterion for grouping? Listen for everyday criteria (size, colour, 'where it lives', 'what we eat') and note which learners mention structure or body features. Note learners who think grouping is obvious and unambiguous, to challenge in the Explain phase. Tally criteria on the board to use later.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-5, learners observe the organisms closely (outdoors in the school compound or at the display) for about 15 minutes. Each learner first works independently to draw or list the 13 organisms and record at least two observable features for each (e.g., has leaves, has legs, has wings, body covering, way of moving, how it gets food, how it reproduces if known). Then each learner independently groups the organisms using his or her own criteria and writes why each organism was placed in a group. After that, the group compares individual groupings and agrees on one grouping, which they draw on manila paper with a title for each group and a reason for it. Groups handle animals gently and return them to their habitat.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute observation sheets and manila paper and markers. Set safety expectations: 'We observe with our eyes first. We do not touch the mushroom, and we handle the earthworm, snail and lizard gently - they are living things like us.' Circulate and ask probing questions, such as: 'Why did you put the mushroom with the plants? What made you decide that?' and 'Where would you put the moss - with the grass or somewhere else? Why?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Prompt groups that finish early: 'Can you make a different grouping using a different rule?' Do NOT tell them the scientific groups. Make sure each group sticks its manila paper on the wall at the end. Cold-call 3 groups to state the rule they used in one sentence. Use textbook illustrations or pictures for unavailable organisms, and let groups share textbooks.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) - Observe step. Learners gather first-hand evidence from local organisms. Independent classification before group work ensures every learner builds their own ideas, and the clash between individual and group groupings begins to show that criteria matter.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each learner's notebook lists at least 2 features per organism; (2) each learner has an individual grouping with a stated reason; (3) groups' manila papers show clear labelled groups with reasons. Look for misconceptions such as 'a mushroom is a plant because it grows in soil', 'the snail is an insect', or 'a mosquito and a butterfly are different because one is harmful'. Record these on a checklist for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners do a gallery walk, visiting at least 3 other groups' manila paper. At each, they note one similarity and one difference compared with their own grouping on sticky notes or in their notebooks. Back in their groups, they discuss: Why did groups differ? Which rule is best? Could someone in another county use our grouping and get the same result? Learners then Think-Pair-Share their conclusion: 'Why do scientists need a standard system of classification?' They give examples, e.g., a goat and a chicken would be grouped together as 'food' or 'farm animals' by some groups but separated by those using legs, body covering or way of reproducing. They watch a short video clip (if available) or read a textbook section on why organisms are classified, and add to their explanations.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk quietly to another group's work. Find one grouping that is the same as yours and one that is different.' After the gallery walk, ask: 'What did you notice? Which organisms were hardest to place?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Press for reasoning: 'Is grouping by size always reliable? What about the caterpillar that becomes a butterfly?' and 'If a visitor from Kericho used your grouping, would they place the mushroom exactly where you did?' Cold-call 5 learners to share an idea from their pair. Highlight that groupings by colour, size, habitat or usefulness vary and none works for everyone. Then lead the class to state: 'Organisms can be grouped using similarities and differences, but scientists require a standard system of classification based on shared, observable characteristics.' Introduce the term 'classification' and write it on the board. If a video is available, play it for 3-4 minutes; otherwise, ask groups to read the textbook introduction on classification (shared textbooks) and summarise it in 2 sentences. Do not introduce Kingdom names in detail yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share and Gallery Walk - learners compare evidence across groups and construct a shared explanation. Seeing conflicting groupings creates cognitive conflict that motivates the need for a standard system (SEP: Constructing Explanations; Engaging in Argument from Evidence). This completes the POE cycle by comparing predictions with observations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for learners who say: 'The groupings differ because we used different rules' and 'We need the same rules for everyone.' Ask 5 random learners to state in one sentence why a standard system is needed. Indicator of success: at least 75% can state that a standard system uses shared, observable characteristics so anyone anywhere gets the same result. Note any who still say one grouping is simply 'correct' without justification.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their groups and write at least two questions each on sticky notes or strips of paper about classifying organisms. Examples: 'How do scientists decide which features to use?', 'Is a mushroom a plant or an animal?', 'Why do moss and fern look so different from maize?', 'What groups do the mosquito and the butterfly belong to?', 'Are viruses living?' Groups post questions on the DQB under the driving question: 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' The class sorts questions into categories (e.g., characteristics used, plant groups, animal groups, tools for identification, viruses). Learners also connect the KICD inquiry questions: 'How are plants and animals classified?' and 'How are viruses important in nature?'
framework.teacherMoves: Display a large chart titled 'DQB: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' Say: 'Write questions you still have. Questions starting with How or Why are very useful.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask: 'What are you still wondering about these organisms?' Cold-call 4 learners to read one question and place it on the board. Cluster similar questions with the class, asking: 'Which questions go together? What name could we give this group?' Point out the question: 'How do scientists decide which characteristics should be used for classification?' and say we will begin there in Lesson 2. Add the KICD inquiry questions if the class has not raised them. Keep the DQB visible and accessible all unit.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board - learners' own questions give purpose and direction to the unit, make learning visible and allow them to track growing understanding. Sorting questions shows patterns and sequences the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner has contributed at least 1 question. Look at the quality of questions: Are they about features, groups or the process of classification (higher quality) versus recall of names only? Observable indicator: at least 3 question clusters emerge and one links to choosing characteristics. Note respectful listening to others' questions (Respect value).

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners draw an initial model on a half-page of paper or in their notebooks. It shows (1) the 13 organisms, (2) their own best grouping, (3) the rule(s) they used, and (4) a note on where their model might fail for someone else (e.g., 'my grouping by habitat puts the lizard and the earthworm together'). They add a short label such as 'What I still don't know'. They then complete the exit ticket: (a) Write one reason why scientists need a standard system of classification. (b) Give one observable characteristic that could be used to group the maize, bean plant and grass together. (c) Write one question you still have. Models are kept in a folder for revision in Lessons 4 and 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw your best current model of how these organisms can be grouped. You will change it later as you learn more - so it is fine if it is not perfect.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after explaining and invite questions. Circulate and ask: 'What rule are you using? Where does your model not work?' Cold-call 3 learners to share the 'weak point' in their model. Hand out the exit ticket and collect it at the door. Close by naming the next question: 'How do scientists decide which characteristics should be used for classification?' Collect models and store them safely for later revision. Ask learners to carefully return any specimens to where they were found and wash hands.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision (initial model) - learners record their current thinking as a model that includes its limitations. Revisiting it in Lessons 4 and 8 helps them see how their understanding grows with evidence. Exit ticket gives each learner a private way to show understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review models and exit tickets using this checklist: (1) model shows a grouping with a stated rule; (2) learner identifies at least one limitation; (3) exit ticket gives a reason for a standard system (e.g., 'so everyone groups the same way'); (4) names an observable characteristic (e.g., 'have leaves and roots'); (5) asks a question. Success criterion: 75% meet at least 3 of 5. Sort tickets into 'ready', 'needs a nudge' and 'needs reteaching' groups to plan Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners truly attempt grouping independently before comparing? Which criteria appeared most (size, colour, habitat, usefulness, structure)? Which organisms caused disagreement (mushroom, moss, snail, mosquito)? Did the specimens or pictures work well and were they safe? Did learners using Kiswahili or mother tongue participate more? What misconceptions need to be addressed in Lesson 2 (e.g., mushroom as a plant, snail as an insect)? Did every learner contribute a question to the DQB? How will I use the exit ticket results to adjust the start of Lesson 2?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed 13 local organisms (maize, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) and noted that they differ in structure, size, body covering, movement and reproduction. Different groups sorted them in different ways (by size, colour, habitat, usefulness).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Organisms can be grouped using similarities and differences, but groupings made with different rules do not agree. Scientists need a standard system of classification based on shared, observable characteristics.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because everyone chose different rules, no single grouping worked for everyone. A standard system uses the same observable characteristics so that any person anywhere can identify and study an organism and get the same result. We still need to find out how scientists decide which characteristics to use.

video.title: Plants: Classification, Reproduction, and Evolution - Overview

LESSONS.title: Kingdom Plantae — Bryophyta
LESSONS.aresKeywords: Bryophyta, moss, liverwort, rhizoid, capsule, sporophyte, gametophyte, spores, non-vascular, Plantae, labelled drawing

slo.purpose: Learners gather evidence that bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) have distinctive shared characteristics that separate them from other plant groups, and use that evidence to improve their classification of the school-environment organisms (moss, fern, maize, bean, grass) and advance the driving question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to outline the general characteristics of organisms in Division Bryophyta: small size, no true roots, stems or leaves, rhizoids for anchorage, no vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), need for moist habitats, spore-bearing capsules on stalks, and dependence of the sporophyte on the gametophyte.
slo.skills: Observing with a hand lens; recording similarities and differences in a table; making an accurate labelled biological drawing with title, scale/magnification, and straight label lines; communicating findings clearly to peers (SEP: Analysing and Interpreting Data; Developing and Using Models).
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the diversity of plants in nature; Respect: be considerate of others' opinions during discussion; Responsibility: care for the environment when collecting specimens; Environmental Conservation: collect only a small amount of moss and return the rest of the habitat undisturbed. Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration - the learner speaks clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of various specimens.
slo.keyInquiry: How are plants and animals classified?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 showed that learners' own groupings (by size, colour, habitat, use as food) conflict and that a standard system based on shared observable characteristics is needed. Lesson 2 gives the first piece of such evidence: one plant group, the bryophytes, can be defined by a set of observable features. This creates the need for Lesson 3: What makes other plants different from bryophytes?
slo.safetyNotes: Collect moss only from safe, accessible damp walls, tree bases, or shaded ground within the school compound; do not climb or go near drains, deep water, or snake-prone long grass. Take only a small patch and replace the rest. Wash hands after handling specimens and soil. Do not taste any plant or mushroom. Hand lenses must never be used to look at the sun. If a learner has allergies to moulds or spores, they should record data rather than handle specimens.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the school-environment collection from Lesson 1 (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, mushroom and others) and focus on the moss, which many groups placed with 'grass' or 'small green things'. They predict how moss differs from maize or bean plants, then examine real moss (or pictures and charts where unavailable) with hand lenses, recording similarities and differences in a table and producing a labelled drawing. A gallery walk lets groups compare drawings and findings, and Think-Pair-Share helps them reason about why moss grows only in damp places and stays small. Learners add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their group classification model to include a 'bryophyte' category defined by observable features. The lesson ends by asking: What makes other plants different from bryophytes?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in their Lesson 1 groups of 4-5 with their earlier classification charts of the school organisms (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, etc.). A moss sample, or picture, is shown. On a sheet, each learner privately writes a prediction: 'Is moss more like maize, grass, or fern? What parts does it have (roots, stem, leaves, flowers)? Why does it grow where it does?' They then do a Think-Pair-Share, using Kiswahili or mother tongue if helpful, but write key terms (root, stem, leaf, spore) in English.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the moss and say: 'In Lesson 1 your groups placed this moss in different places. Today we ask: is moss just a very small grass, or is it something different?' Give 1 minute silent writing time. Say: 'Write your prediction and one reason. I will not tell you if you are right yet.' Then say 'Turn to your partner and share.' Allow 2 minutes. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking 'Where on the school compound did we find moss and what does that tell us?' before taking responses. Cold-call 3 learners from different groups using the roll book, not volunteers, and record their predictions on the board under 'Our predictions' without judging them. Ask: 'Who has a different idea?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: Making predictions before observation reveals learners' existing ideas (e.g. that moss has roots and flowers like maize) and creates a reason to look carefully. Pair sharing lets every learner rehearse ideas before whole-class talk, so they are invested in checking their prediction against evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check prediction sheets while circulating. Look for: (1) a prediction that names at least two plant parts; (2) a reason linked to an earlier observation; (3) any misconception such as 'moss has roots and flowers' or 'moss is a fungus like mushroom'. Tally on the board how many predict moss is 'like grass', 'like fern', or 'different from both' to revisit after observation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners collect a small, teacher-approved patch of moss from a damp shaded area near the school (or receive prepared specimens, pictures, charts and textbook illustrations where moss is unavailable; a short video may be used if available but is not required). Using hand lenses, they examine: the overall size and colour; the leaf-like structures (are they thin, one cell thick, with veins?); the stem-like structure; the thread-like rhizoids at the base and whether there are real roots; and, where present, the stalk and spore capsule. They compare with a maize or bean seedling (and a fern frond if available) to record similarities and differences in a table with columns: Feature | Moss | Maize/Bean | Fern. They measure heights with a ruler, note the habitat (damp, shaded, wall, tree trunk), and then make a labelled drawing of one moss plant, with a title, magnification, and label lines for rhizoids, 'stem', 'leaf-like structures', stalk and capsule (if present).
framework.teacherMoves: Before going out, state the safety and conservation rules: 'Take only a small patch the size of your palm, put the rest back, and stay within the marked area.' Give each group a hand lens, a ruler, a plastic bag or tray, and a data table. Circulate and ask: 'What do you see at the base of the moss? Is that the same as the maize root? How do you know?' and 'What do you notice about the thickness of the leaves?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Prompt for evidence: 'Show me on the specimen.' Model drawing skills briefly: 'Use a sharp pencil, single clear lines, no shading, label lines must not cross.' If groups lack specimens, give each a picture or chart and ask them to point out features using the textbook. Allow groups to share textbooks. Ask 2 groups to report what they found most surprising.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation with data table and scientific drawing: Comparing moss side by side with maize, bean and fern makes learners focus on shared, observable features instead of size or colour alone. Recording evidence in a table converts observations into data that can be used for classification, building the idea that groups are defined by sets of characteristics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners: (1) use hand lenses correctly and refer to specific structures; (2) record at least four differences between moss and maize/bean in the table (e.g. rhizoids vs true roots, no flowers, small size, no vascular tissue visible, spore capsule vs seeds); (3) produce a drawing with title, magnification, accurate proportions and neat label lines. Use a 3-point checklist (Meets / Partly / Not yet) and note groups needing support.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups display their labelled drawings and tables around the room for a gallery walk. Each learner visits at least three other groups' displays with sticky notes, leaving one 'Star' (something accurate or well labelled) and one 'Question' (something unclear). Back in their group, learners read the feedback and revise their drawings. Then, in Think-Pair-Share, they answer: 'Why does moss stay small and grow only in damp places? How does it reproduce without seeds or flowers?' Using their observations and the textbook, they write an explanation that lists the characteristics of Division Bryophyta: no vascular tissue (no xylem and phloem), rhizoids instead of true roots, thin leaf-like structures, spores produced in capsules, and need for water for fertilisation. They return to their predictions and mark them as supported, partly supported or changed.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Leave your drawing on the desk and walk quietly. Read the labels and tables and give feedback using the Star and Question format.' Allow 8 minutes for the gallery walk. Then ask: 'Which features did every group find in moss?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners from different groups. Record agreed characteristics on the board as 'Class evidence'. Pose: 'Maize carries water up through its stem. What does moss do without xylem and phloem? What does that tell us about its size and where it can live?' Give 2 minutes for Think-Pair-Share, then cold-call 3 pairs. Introduce key terms (Bryophyta, rhizoids, spores, capsule) only after learners describe the features in their own words. Address misconceptions: 'Rhizoids anchor the plant and do not transport water like true roots.' Link to Kenya: 'Where have you seen moss near home, on rocks near Kericho tea estates or damp walls in Nairobi? What is common about those places?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery walk with Think-Pair-Share: Peer feedback exposes differences in how groups interpret the same structures and pushes them to justify their labelling with evidence. Connecting structure (no vascular tissue, rhizoids) to function (small size, moist habitat) turns a list of facts into an explanation, making the classification meaningful instead of memorised.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for learners who: (1) explain moss's small size and damp habitat by referring to the lack of vascular tissue and the need for water; (2) correctly distinguish rhizoids from true roots; (3) revise their prediction with evidence. Use thumbs up/sideways/down on 'I can list three characteristics of bryophytes' and follow up with learners who show sideways or down. Collect the Star and Question sticky notes to identify common errors.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the central question: 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' Each group writes on sticky notes (1) one thing they have learned about moss and bryophytes that helps classification and (2) one new question, for example 'Do ferns have roots like maize?', 'What makes bean plants different from moss?', 'How do plants with seeds reproduce?' They place notes on the board under headings such as 'What we learned', 'New questions' and 'Still not sure', and group similar questions with the teacher.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the Driving Question Board. Today we added evidence about one group of plants. What can we now say, and what do we still need to find out?' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before inviting contributions. Cold-call 3 groups to read out and place one question each. Sort questions with the class: 'Which questions are about other plants? Which about animals? Which about viruses?' Highlight the question 'What makes other plants different from bryophytes?' and circle it as the focus for Lesson 3. Praise question quality: 'This question asks for evidence we can gather - that is a strong scientific question.' Ensure respectful tone: 'We value each person's ideas.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: Collecting learner-generated questions makes the unit's direction visible and shows that new evidence raises new questions. Sorting questions by type helps learners see how today's work on one plant group connects to the larger need for a standard classification system.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sticky notes (1) state a learned idea supported by evidence from today (e.g. 'Moss has no true roots, only rhizoids'); (2) contain at least one researchable question; and (3) are linked to the driving question. Note learners who cannot yet generate questions, and pair them with stronger peers next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups revisit their Lesson 1 classification model (chart of maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat). They revise it by creating a 'Bryophyta' category for moss based on the shared observable features gathered today, and write the criteria beside it (e.g. 'small, no true roots, stem or leaves, rhizoids, no vascular tissue, spores in capsule, grows in damp places'). They mark where other organisms (maize, bean, grass, fern) still do not fit and need more evidence. Individually, learners complete an exit ticket summarising the lesson in the Observed / Learned / Explained table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Lesson 1 model. Using today's evidence, what must change? Add a group for moss and write the features that decide membership.' Circulate and ask: 'Which feature is the most useful for telling moss apart from maize? Why is colour not a good feature?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to share a revised part of their model, and ask others: 'Do you agree? What evidence supports that?' Point out that scientists in Kenya, such as botanists at the National Museums of Kenya herbarium, use shared characteristics like these to name and group plants. Close with: 'We now know what defines bryophytes. What do you think makes other plants, like ferns and maize, different? That is our question for the next lesson.' Distribute the exit ticket.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: Updating the classification model with evidence shows learners how scientific ideas change as data accumulate. Writing explicit criteria for a group moves learners from sorting by appearance or usefulness toward using shared, observable characteristics, which advances the unit's driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that revised models (1) include a labelled Bryophyta group with at least three observable criteria; (2) avoid non-scientific criteria (size alone, colour, usefulness); and (3) show where unresolved organisms remain. Review exit tickets: successful responses cite at least two bryophyte characteristics and one evidence-based reason for moss's habitat. Use results to plan support for Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners explained moss's small size and damp habitat using evidence (no vascular tissue, rhizoids) rather than just recalling facts? Did learners confuse rhizoids with true roots, or moss with fungi such as mushroom? Were specimens available, or did pictures limit observation of the capsule? How effective was the gallery walk in improving drawing quality and the accuracy of labels? Did groups' revised models move from appearance or use toward shared structural characteristics? Which new questions on the DQB should drive the Lesson 3 evidence-gathering activity on ferns, conifers and flowering plants?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Describe what you observed in the moss with a hand lens: its size, the base (rhizoids), the stem-like and leaf-like parts, any spore capsules, where it was growing, and how it differed from maize or bean plants.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: State the characteristics that identify Division Bryophyta (e.g. small size, rhizoids instead of true roots, no vascular tissue, spores in capsules, damp habitats) and how they differ from other plants.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain why moss stays small and grows in damp places, and how this evidence helps scientists classify plants more accurately than grouping by size, colour or use. What new question do you now have about how other plants differ from bryophytes?

LESSONS.title: Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
LESSONS.aresKeywords: Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta, fern, sorus, spores, seeds, vascular tissue, true roots, frond, monocot, dicot, comparison table, Jigsaw, Gallery walk

slo.purpose: Learners gather evidence from real plants (fern, maize, bean) to show that pteridophytes and spermatophytes have features that distinguish them from bryophytes and from each other, and use it to improve their class model of how organisms are grouped.
slo.knowledge: a) outline the general characteristics of organisms in Divisions Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta. Pteridophytes (ferns) have true roots, stems and leaves (fronds) with vascular tissue and reproduce by spores in sori, with no seeds or flowers. Spermatophytes have true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue and reproduce by seeds (in cones or flowers). Bryophytes (moss) lack true roots and vascular tissue.
slo.skills: Observing and recording structures of roots, stems, leaves and reproductive parts; comparing and contrasting specimens; constructing a comparison table; (NGSS SEP) analysing and interpreting data, and developing and using models; Communication and Collaboration: speaking clearly to peers while discussing the distinguishing characteristics of various specimens.
slo.attitudes: e) appreciate the diversity of plants and animals in nature. Respect: considerate of others' opinions during group discussion. Responsibility: cares for the environment while collecting specimens. PCI Environmental Conservation: collects only small samples responsibly and leaves the habitat intact.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How are plants and animals classified?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 showed that learners' own groupings (size, colour, use) conflict, and that moss (Bryophyta) is grouped by structural features. In Lesson 3 learners see that features such as vascular tissue, spores versus seeds, and flowers separate more plant groups. This raises the next question: 'How can we classify plants systematically when we encounter an unknown plant?', which leads to the dichotomous key work in Lesson 4.
slo.safetyNotes: Collect only small samples (one frond, one seedling) from the school compound, with teacher permission. Do not collect unknown plants, and do not taste any plant or mushroom. Wash hands after handling soil and plants. Avoid plants with thorns or irritant sap, such as euphorbia. Use hand lenses carefully and never look at the sun. Pull up bean or maize seedlings gently and return waste to the compost pit.

LESSONS.overview: Back to our phenomenon: the maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom and other organisms from the school compound are all living, but our own groupings by size, colour or use disagree. Today learners focus on the plants. They predict how a fern differs from moss and from maize or beans, then examine real fern fronds (with sori on the underside), maize and bean seedlings or plants (or pictures where specimens are unavailable). Working in Jigsaw expert groups (roots, stems, leaves, reproductive structures), they gather evidence, return to home groups to build a comparison table of Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta, then take a Gallery walk to compare tables and resolve differences. A short video (Video 2) or chart supports the observations but is not essential if there is no internet. Learners add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their class model of plant grouping, ending with the new question: how do we classify an unknown plant systematically?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the compound organisms from the phenomenon (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss). On a card each writes a prediction: 'How will a fern differ from moss, and from a maize or bean plant? Think about roots, stems, leaves and how they make new plants.' They think alone for 2 minutes, then pair and share, drawing a quick sketch of what they expect to see on the underside of a fern frond. Kiswahili may be used for discussion; key terms are written in English.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up a fern frond, a maize plant and a bean plant beside the moss from Lesson 2. Say: 'We said earlier that our own groups did not agree. Today we ask what features of these plants everyone could check.' Ask: 'Which of these has real roots? Which makes seeds? How do you know?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before anyone speaks. Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions, and ask 2 of them: 'What makes you think so?' Record predictions on the board under 'Our Predictions' without correcting them. Remind learners: 'A prediction is our best idea, not a right or wrong answer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think–Pair–Share (with the Predict stage of POE): individual thinking exposes prior ideas (for example 'all green plants make seeds', 'ferns are flowering plants'), and pairing lets learners test ideas aloud, so the investigation has a purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 3 of 5 learners' cards include a feature (roots, seeds, spores, flowers) rather than just size or colour; (2) learners give a reason with 'because'; (3) note common misconceptions on the board, such as 'ferns have flowers' or 'moss has roots'. Use a tally of misconceptions to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Jigsaw, Part 1 (expert groups, 20 minutes): Class is split into 4 expert groups: Roots, Stems, Leaves, and Reproductive structures. Each group examines a fern, a maize plant and a bean plant (and the moss from Lesson 2 for comparison), using hand lenses and, where needed, drawings or pictures from the textbook or charts. Roots: fibrous (maize) vs tap root (bean) vs rhizome with fibrous roots (fern) vs rhizoids (moss). Stems: rhizome in fern, herbaceous stems with vascular bundles in maize and bean. Leaves: fronds with pinnae (fern); long narrow leaves with parallel veins (maize); broad leaves with net veins (bean). Reproductive: brown sori on the underside of a fern frond (spores); maize cob and tassel (flowers, grains); bean flowers and pods with seeds. Learners record observations in labelled sketches and notes. Jigsaw, Part 2 (home groups, 15 minutes): Learners regroup so each home group has one expert from every topic; each expert teaches the others, and the group builds a comparison table: Feature | Bryophyta (moss) | Pteridophyta (fern) | Spermatophyta (maize, bean). Where no fern is available, use charts or Video 2, and pause the video at key points for learners to record notes.
framework.teacherMoves: Set up stations before class. Safety reminder: 'Handle plants gently, take only what I give you, and wash your hands afterwards.' Circulate and ask: 'What do you see on the underside of the fern frond? How is it different from the bean leaf?' and 'Where are the seeds in the bean? Where would you look for seeds in the fern?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Prompt without telling: 'Count the veins. Do they run parallel or form a net?' Cold-call 2 experts per group in Part 2 to explain their findings: 'Tell your group one thing you saw and one piece of evidence.' Make sure each group has one fully completed table. If Video 2 is used, play it once for 3-4 minutes, say: 'Watch for spores and seeds. Note down two things you did not see in the specimens,' then pause to share in pairs.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Jigsaw cooperative learning: each learner becomes responsible for a piece of evidence and must explain it to others, so every learner contributes to the final table and builds understanding of the characteristics. Building a comparison table organises observations into patterns across groups.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: expert sketches show correct labels (for example sori, frond, tap root, fibrous roots); learners use words like 'spores' and 'seeds' in explanations; each home group table has all 4 features for all 3 divisions; learners can state at least one feature that separates ferns from moss (true roots, vascular tissue) and ferns from seed plants (spores, no seeds). Use a checklist during circulation.

framework.learnerExperience: Gallery walk (12 minutes): Each home group posts its comparison table on the wall. Groups rotate every 2 minutes, using sticky notes to add a star (a strong piece of evidence), a question mark (unclear), or a suggestion. Back at their own tables, groups revise them. Then in a class discussion learners revisit predictions and answer: 'What features separate Pteridophyta from Bryophyta? What separates Spermatophyta from Pteridophyta?' They explain using evidence: ferns have vascular tissue, true roots and fronds but reproduce by spores in sori; spermatophytes have vascular tissue and reproduce by seeds (in flowers or cones). They notice maize and bean differ too (parallel vs net veins, fibrous vs tap root), hinting at monocots and dicots for later. Learners write 2-3 sentences in their notebooks: 'The feature that best separates a fern from a bean plant is ___ because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk like scientists. Look for evidence, not just opinions. Where do tables agree? Where do they disagree?' Ask during the walk: 'Which feature appears in every table? Why would scientists use this feature rather than colour or size?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners after the walk: 'What did you change in your table and why?' Probe the misconceptions from the Predict phase: 'Earlier some of us said ferns have flowers. What does the evidence say?' Introduce terms only after learners use their own words: spores, sori, vascular tissue, fronds, seeds. Link back to the phenomenon: 'Remember our groups by size or by use as food? Would a farmer in Kericho and a student in Kisumu both be able to check spores and seeds?' Mention Kenyan examples: bracken fern in Aberdare forests, maize and beans (githeri) as spermatophytes, and Kenyan scientist Prof. Wangari Maathai's tree planting for conservation (trees are spermatophytes).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery walk with Claim–Evidence–Reasoning prompts: comparing the work of other groups exposes differences, makes learners justify claims with observed evidence and builds consensus on shared, observable characteristics, which is the basis of classification.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebook sentences: look for (1) a correct feature, (2) evidence from specimens, (3) a reason linking to classification. Success criteria: at least 80% of learners name spores vs seeds correctly. Look for sticky notes that give constructive feedback. Identify learners who still confuse ferns with flowering plants for follow-up with a diagram.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' They write new questions on sticky notes based on today's work, for example: 'Why do ferns need damp places?', 'How do we tell a maize plant from grass?', 'What about plants with cones, like cypress?', 'How do we classify a plant when we do not know it?' They place the notes under categories (Plants, Animals, Method, Viruses) and mark one that they think can be answered next lesson. They also move or tick questions answered today, such as 'How is moss different from a fern?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of our questions did today's evidence help to answer? What new questions came up?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask each pair to write at least one question. Cold-call 3 pairs to read out and place questions, asking: 'Why does that question belong there?' Highlight the question that links to the next lesson: 'How can we classify plants systematically when we encounter an unknown plant?' Praise questions that need evidence and not just yes/no answers. Accept Kiswahili questions and translate key terms into English with the class.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: it makes learners' thinking visible, connects each lesson to the anchoring phenomenon, and shows progress and gaps, driving the need for the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: each pair contributes at least one question; at least half the questions refer to features or methods (not just facts); some questions show links between divisions or ask about unknown plants. Record question types (what, why, how) to plan the next lesson, and tick off answered questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model (a flow chart or concept map) that shows how organisms from the school environment can be grouped. They add Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta next to Bryophyta, and draw the features used at each branch, for example: Vascular tissue? No: Bryophyta (moss). Yes: Seeds? No, spores: Pteridophyta (fern). Yes, seeds: Spermatophyta (maize, bean). In groups, they add the maize, bean, grass, fern and moss from the phenomenon into the model and note which ones are still unclear (for example mushroom, which is not a plant). Each learner completes a summary table in their notebook (What we observed / What we learned / How it helps explain the phenomenon) and notes one limit of the model: 'It does not yet tell us how to identify an unknown plant step by step.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our first groups did not agree. Now, using features anyone can observe, where do our plants go? Show me on the model.' Draw the model skeleton and let groups add labels. Ask: 'What evidence supports this branch? What is missing?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to place one organism and justify it. Ask: 'Where would the mushroom go? Why not here?' (leave unresolved; it is revisited in Lesson 8). Close with: 'If a farmer in Rift Valley brings you an unknown plant, what would you check first? How could we make this a step-by-step tool?' and introduce Lesson 4: dichotomous keys. Collect model sketches as an exit ticket.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: updating the class model with new evidence helps learners organise features into a hierarchy and see why a standard, shared system works better than personal groupings, and it exposes the limits that lead to dichotomous keys.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the model correctly places moss, fern, and maize/bean using spores vs seeds and vascular tissue; learners justify at least one placement with evidence; the exit ticket names one limitation of the model. Use a 3-level rubric (placement correct, evidence stated, limitation identified) to decide who needs extra support with diagrams or reteaching before Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did every learner handle real specimens or clear pictures and contribute to the Jigsaw? Which misconceptions (ferns have flowers, moss has roots, all plants have seeds) remained after the Gallery walk? Was WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds used consistently, and did quieter learners speak when cold-called? Were specimens (ferns) available locally, or did I rely on pictures, and how did this affect learners' evidence? Did learners connect their table back to the phenomenon and our conflicting groupings? What should I adjust for Lesson 4 (dichotomous key challenge) based on the DQB questions?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that ferns have true roots, a rhizome and fronds with brown sori on the underside, while maize and bean plants have roots, stems, leaves and flowers that produce seeds (grains and pods). Moss has no true roots and no vascular tissue.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Pteridophytes reproduce by spores and have vascular tissue but no seeds or flowers; spermatophytes reproduce by seeds and have vascular tissue; bryophytes lack vascular tissue and true roots. These are shared, observable features anyone can check.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: These features help explain our phenomenon because they give everyone the same rules for grouping plants, instead of personal groupings by size, colour or use as food. We still need a step-by-step way to identify an unknown plant.

LESSONS.title: Using Dichotomous Keys
LESSONS.aresKeywords: dichotomous key, contrasting characteristics, couplet, identification, monocot, dicot, fern, moss, specimen, classification

slo.purpose: Learners figure out that a dichotomous key uses pairs of contrasting, observable characteristics to identify organisms. They use this idea to improve the school-organism classification models they started in earlier lessons, so that anyone can identify an organism and get the same answer.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) construct and use dichotomous keys to identify various plants (KICD: construct and use dichotomous keys to identify various plants and animals); (2) state the principles of constructing a dichotomous key: paired contrasting statements, observable features, one clear choice at each step, numbered couplets; (3) relate the key to the distinguishing features of Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta, and of monocots and dicots.
slo.skills: NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models (revising the group classification model into a key); Analyzing and Interpreting Data (comparing the results of different users of the same key); Constructing Explanations (explaining why a key gives the same answer for every user). Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration (speaking clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics); Creativity and Imagination (trying varied ideas while designing the key).
slo.attitudes: Values: Respect (being considerate of others' opinions when groups disagree on a feature) and Responsibility (caring for the environment while collecting plants). PCI: Environmental Conservation (collecting only small samples responsibly and leaving the habitat undisturbed). Appreciating the diversity of plants in the local environment.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question 1: How are plants and animals classified? Driving question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1-3 learners saw that their own groupings (size, colour, habitat, usefulness as food) differ between groups, and they met the shared characteristics of plant divisions. Lesson 4 gives them a tool that turns those observable characteristics into a step-by-step identification method that any person gets the same answer from. It ends with the question: Can the same method be used to identify animals? This leads to Lesson 5.
slo.safetyNotes: Collect only plants that are common and known (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, sukuma wiki, Mexican marigold). Avoid unknown plants, thorny or irritating plants (e.g. nettle), and wild mushrooms; mushrooms are used only as pictures. Wash hands after handling soil and plants. Take only one leaf or small sample per plant; do not uproot plants. Move in groups, stay within the school compound. Use rulers carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the school-organism phenomenon: 'If all these organisms are living things, how can scientists organise them so that any person anywhere can identify them?' Groups first predict whether two different people could use the same set of written steps to name the same plant. They then study a sample key, use it on local plants (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, sukuma wiki leaf) and see that different groups reach the same answer, which is different from their earlier personal groupings. In the Explain phase they use Think-Pair-Share to figure out the rules of a good key and complete the Dichotomous-key Challenge of building a key for their own collected plant specimens. They add the new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their classification model from earlier lessons. Activities need no internet. Prepared keys, specimens and worksheets are used; photographs or drawings replace any missing specimen. Discussion may begin in Kiswahili or mother tongue, while scientific terms are recorded in English.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners sit in their groups of 4-5 with the group classification charts they made in earlier lessons (grouped by size, colour, habitat, food use). The teacher holds up a maize plant and a fern and asks: 'Imagine a farmer in Kericho wants to name this plant, but you are not there. Could you write instructions so that she gets the same name you do?' Individually, learners write a prediction in their notebooks: 'I think instructions for identifying plants should look like...' and sketch or list the first two steps they would write. They then share in pairs (Think-Pair-Share), using Kiswahili if helpful, and record a short agreed prediction on the group chart: 'Our key will work if...'
framework.teacherMoves: Display the maize plant, fern, bean plant and moss on the front table. Say: 'In Lesson 1 your groups sorted these organisms in different ways, and the groups did not agree. Today we ask: how can any person anywhere get the same name for the same organism?' Give 1 minute silent think time. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking 'What would make the instructions work for everyone?' before taking any answer. Cold-call 3 pairs (not volunteers) to read their predictions aloud. Say: 'I am not looking for the right answer yet; I want your best prediction.' Write 3 predictions on the board, circle common words (e.g. 'leaf', 'flower', 'yes/no'). Do not reveal the term dichotomous key yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Predict step) combined with Think-Pair-Share. Predicting before instruction exposes learners' preconceptions (e.g. that grouping by colour or size is enough) and gives a baseline that learners will compare with evidence later. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner thinking time and a chance to rehearse ideas before whole-class talk.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) predictions that mention observable features (leaf shape, presence of flowers, seeds, roots) rather than opinions (useful, pretty); (2) at least 3 of the cold-called pairs mention that steps must be clear or have only two choices; (3) number of learners who still suggest size or colour as the only basis. Tally on a class list: 'observable feature / opinion / no response'. Note groups who need support at the Observe stage.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A (8 min): Each group receives a prepared sample key for six local plants, worksheets and rulers. They read the first couplet together (e.g. 1a: Plant has no true roots, stems or leaves; 1b: Plant has true roots, stems and leaves), and the teacher models it with moss. Part B (17 min): Groups go outside or to a specimen table (plant specimens, photographs or drawings where plants are missing) with maize, bean plant, grass, fern, moss and sukuma wiki. Using the key, a ruler and observation, they identify each unknown specimen labelled A-F, recording the path taken through the couplets (e.g. 1b to 2a to 3b) and the final name. They measure features that need numbers (e.g. leaf length, number of leaf veins or petals) with rulers. Groups swap and a second member repeats the key on one specimen to see whether the answer matches. They note disagreements and which statement caused them.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first couplet aloud with moss: 'Does it have true roots, stems and leaves? Look carefully, then choose one statement.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which two statements are you choosing between? What do you see that tells you?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each question before prompting. Avoid telling them the plant name; instead say 'Show me your path through the key.' Cold-call 2 learners per group to explain one choice. Remind learners: 'Collect only a small piece; do not pull up the whole plant', and 'Wash your hands afterwards.' Ask groups that finish early: 'Where did your partner choose differently from you? Why?' Use photographs for any plants unavailable, and tell learners that mushrooms are observed from pictures only.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Observe step) with the Dichotomous-key Challenge. Using a ready-made key on real local specimens lets learners experience that the same steps give the same answer, which directly tests their earlier prediction and shows the difference from their own unstructured groupings. Paired verification builds evidence from repeated trials.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) group records a complete path through the key for at least 5 of 6 specimens; (2) learners point to the actual feature on the specimen when justifying a choice; (3) rulers are used correctly (zero-end alignment, units recorded); (4) the second user of the key reaches the same name for at least 4 of 6 specimens. Use a checklist while circulating. Record which couplets caused disagreements for use in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Step 1 (8 min) Think-Pair-Share: Learners compare results with their prediction and answer: 'Why did the key give the same answer to different people when our earlier groupings did not?' Step 2 (7 min): Pairs study the sample key and list what makes each couplet good (two contrasting statements, observable features, one choice only, no opinions such as 'useful' or 'beautiful', numbered). Whole class builds a shared list of principles of construction. Step 3 (10 min) Dichotomous-key Challenge: Each group takes 4 plants they collected or were given (e.g. maize, bean, fern, moss, grass or sukuma wiki) and writes a simple key with at least 3 couplets using visible features (e.g. parallel veins versus net veins, fronds versus broad leaves, presence of seeds). They swap keys with another group, which tries to identify the specimens with it and gives feedback: 'Which couplet was unclear?' Groups then revise their key. Learners link their features to the divisions: moss (Bryophyta), fern (Pteridophyta), maize and grass (monocots), bean and sukuma wiki (dicots) in Spermatophyta.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Why did the key give the same answer to different people, when your earlier groupings did not?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 pairs. Press for reasoning: 'Which feature was a better choice than colour? Why?' Challenge weak couplets: 'Is that statement something we can see and measure, or is it an opinion?' Write learners' principles on the board and add missing ones with the KICD wording (principles of construction, identification of organisms). During the challenge, circulate with the prompt: 'Could someone from Mombasa who has never seen this plant use your key?' Build in respect: remind groups to give feedback kindly and to listen to others' ideas ('First say one thing that works well, then one suggestion'). Connect back to the phenomenon: 'Our school organisms are all living things, yet this method lets anyone name them.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share, then a Dichotomous-key Challenge with peer testing. Explaining why the key works converts observations into an understanding of the concept (contrasting pairs, observable features). Constructing a key for their own specimens and having another group test it applies the concept and uses peer feedback to build accuracy, in line with the NGSS practice of constructing explanations and revising models.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) learners state that a good couplet contains two contrasting, observable statements; (2) keys have at least 3 numbered couplets that lead to a single name for every specimen; (3) the swapping group correctly identifies at least 3 of 4 specimens; (4) learners correctly link at least two features to the division or class (e.g. parallel veins = monocot; spores/fronds = fern). Use a quick rubric (3 = key works without help, 2 = one unclear couplet, 1 = key needs reteaching). Misconceptions to note: using size/colour as the only basis, or writing statements with more than two choices.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners return to the class Driving Question Board headed 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?'. On sticky notes, each group writes (a) one thing they now understand about identifying plants (e.g. 'A key uses pairs of opposite features'), and (b) one new question (e.g. 'Can the same method be used to identify animals?', 'What if an organism fits neither choice?', 'How do we key organisms such as a mosquito or an earthworm?'). Groups place notes under the headings 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New questions' and read other groups' notes during a short walk around the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Choose one question that you think our next lesson should investigate.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds of silent writing before notes go up. Cold-call 3 groups to read one note and explain where it belongs. Move answered notes only after asking the class: 'What evidence from today shows this question is answered?' Highlight the question 'Can the same method be used to identify animals?' as the bridge to Lesson 5, and link it to the phenomenon: 'We have a method for plants in our school, but what about the mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat?' Acknowledge and value all questions respectfully.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board. The DQB makes learning visible over the unit, so learners see how today's evidence answers earlier questions and generates new ones. This keeps the unit phenomenon-driven by letting students' questions guide the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) each group posts at least one 'what we learned' and one new question; (2) at least half of the questions refer to animals or exceptions to a key; (3) learners can justify the position of a note using evidence from the key activity. Record questions that reveal confusion (e.g. 'Is a key the same as a table of groups?') for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Groups take out their classification model from Lessons 1-3 (chart or diagram of the school organisms, including their original grouping and any added division/class features). They revise it by (1) adding the dichotomous key they built as a 'tool for identification' alongside their groups; (2) crossing out or relabelling groupings based on opinion or unreliable features (e.g. 'good to eat'); (3) adding arrows linking observable features to the groups (Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, monocots, dicots); and (4) writing a short caption: 'Our model now explains that organisms can be identified accurately because...'. They mark with a different colour what changed and why, and leave a box labelled 'Animals: still to be tested'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your model from last lesson. What can it now explain that it could not before? What still does not work?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before groups begin. Circulate and ask each group: 'Which piece of evidence from today made you change this part of the model?' Cold-call 2 groups to share one revision. Prompt: 'Does your model show why two people using the same key get the same name?' Collect models for display and use in the Lesson 8 final model. Link ahead: 'Next lesson we ask whether the same method works for the animals on our school list.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision. Updating the model with new evidence helps learners see classification as a developing explanation, not a list of facts. Colour-coding revisions makes their thinking visible and gives evidence of conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) the model shows the key as a step-by-step tool and not just groups; (2) at least two revisions are tied to evidence (a feature or result from the activity); (3) captions use terms such as contrasting, observable, couplet, monocot, dicot; (4) a 'still to be tested' box for animals is present. Use a 3-point rubric: complete revision with evidence, partial revision, no revision.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: Did learners use observable features (leaf veins, fronds, seeds) rather than opinions when making choices? Which couplets caused disagreements, and why? Did every learner (including those who used Kiswahili first) contribute to building the key? Were specimens, photographs or drawings enough for all groups? Did collection of plants stay responsible and minimal? Which learners still rely on size or colour to classify, and how will you support them in Lesson 5 when keys are applied to animals? Record the questions on the DQB that will guide the next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We used a sample dichotomous key and a ruler to identify local plants (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, sukuma wiki) and found that different group members reached the same name when they followed the same couplets.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A dichotomous key uses pairs of contrasting, observable characteristics, in numbered couplets, so that each step has only two choices and leads to one identification. Features such as true roots, stems and leaves, fronds, seeds, and parallel versus net veins help place plants into Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta (monocots and dicots).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: A key gives the same answer to everyone because it uses clear, observable features rather than personal opinions such as size, colour or usefulness. This is how scientists can organise the organisms around our school so that anyone can identify them. New question: can the same method be used to identify animals?

LESSONS.title: Kingdom Animalia — major phyla
LESSONS.aresKeywords: Kingdom Animalia, phylum, Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Chordata, body symmetry, segmentation, exoskeleton, backbone, Claim-Evidence-Reasoning

slo.purpose: Learners use observable body features of animals from the school environment to group them into major phyla and justify their placement, advancing the unit question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?
slo.knowledge: Specific learning outcome: By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to: c) classify organisms into phyla and classes of Kingdom Animalia. Learners recognise that animals are grouped into phyla using body features such as symmetry, body segmentation, presence of a backbone, type of body covering, and jointed limbs. They link Annelida (earthworm), Mollusca (snail), Arthropoda (mosquito, butterfly) and Chordata (chicken, lizard, goat) to the organisms in the phenomenon.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: Analysing and interpreting data (recording body features in a table); Constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; Engaging in argument from evidence (justifying phylum placement); Developing and using models (revising the class classification model). Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration - the learner speaks clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of various specimens. Creativity and Imagination.
slo.attitudes: Values: Respect - the learner is considerate of others' opinions while discussing groupings. Responsibility - the learner cares for the environment while collecting specimens. PCI - Animal Welfare: the learner handles animals with care while observing and grouping them using distinguishing characteristics. PCI - Environmental Conservation.
