Appreciate the diversity of plants and animals in nature.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry question: How are plants and animals classified? Lesson question: What body features allow us to place the animals we found around our school into major phyla, and how do we defend our choices with evidence?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-4 showed that groupings by size, colour or usefulness differ between groups and that scientists use shared, observable characteristics, including Kingdom Plantae divisions. Lesson 5 turns to the animals in the phenomenon (mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat). It gives learners the evidence that animals can be sorted by body plan and leads to the next question: How are animals within the same phylum further classified?
slo.safetyNotes: Handle live animals gently and return them to where they were found (Animal Welfare). Do not collect or touch unknown, venomous or dangerous organisms such as snakes, scorpions, bees or wasps, or stinging caterpillars. Use preserved specimens, dead insects or pictures where live ones are not available. Wash hands with soap after handling soil, earthworms, snails or specimens. Wear gloves for snails and earthworms if available. Do not taste anything. Keep mosquitoes as pictures or dead specimens only. Return all organisms to the school garden after observation.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon: the maize, beans, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat around the school. After Lessons 1-4 they know groupings by colour or size disagree and scientists use shared observable features. In this lesson they focus on the animals. They first predict how they would group the eight animals, then observe specimens or pictures (earthworm, snail, grasshopper or butterfly, mosquito, tilapia or omena from Lake Victoria, lizard, chicken, goat) in expert Jigsaw groups looking at body symmetry, segmentation, shell, exoskeleton, jointed legs, backbone and body covering. They then return to home groups, teach each other, and complete a Gallery Walk of grouped specimens. They write Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statements to justify phylum placement, add new questions to the Driving Question Board, and revise their class classification model. The lesson ends with the question: if the goat and the chicken are both Chordata, how do we tell them apart? This leads to Lesson 6. Learners may discuss in Kiswahili or their mother tongue, while scientific terms are recorded in English. The lesson works without internet; the video is optional.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the school-yard organisms from the phenomenon. In groups of 4 they receive picture cards or real safe specimens of the animals only: earthworm, snail, mosquito, butterfly, chicken, lizard, goat, plus tilapia or omena. Individually they write a prediction: 'I think the animals can be grouped into ___ groups because ___.' Then they Think-Pair-Share with a partner and sort the cards into their own groups on a sheet of manila paper, labelling the rule they used. Sorting rules are recorded on the board. Learners may use Kiswahili to discuss, e.g. 'wanyama wenye mgongo' and 'wasio na mgongo'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember our puzzle: if all these are living things, how can anyone anywhere organise them so that they can be identified? Today we look only at the animals.' Display the picture cards. Ask: 'Before we learn any new names, how would YOU group these eight animals? Write your prediction silently.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before pairs talk. Circulate and listen for rules such as size, habitat, 'those we eat', 'those that fly'. Cold-call 4 groups to share their rules and write them on the board without judging. Ask: 'Did every group choose the same rule? What problem does that create if a scientist in Nairobi and one in Kisumu need to agree?' Put the sorted sheets aside for the Gallery Walk later.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction before seeing evidence surfaces learners' existing ideas (size, habitat, food use) so they can later compare these with the scientific features. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner a voice, including those who speak in Kiswahili first.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each learner has a written individual prediction with a reason. (2) Groups can state their sorting rule aloud. (3) At least 3 different rules are recorded on the board, showing the problem of non-standard grouping. (4) Learners use words like 'has a backbone' or 'has a shell' unprompted: note who does so. Tally learners who group only by habitat or food use to target in the next phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Jigsaw. Learners form home groups of 5 and each member joins an expert group focusing on one set of specimens or pictures and charts: Expert A: Annelida and Mollusca (earthworm, snail); Expert B: Arthropoda - insects (butterfly, mosquito, grasshopper); Expert C: Arthropoda - others (spider, millipede, crab or prawn picture from Mombasa); Expert D: Chordata - fish and reptiles (tilapia or omena, lizard); Expert E: Chordata - birds and mammals (chicken, goat). Each expert group observes the specimens/pictures, uses textbooks and charts, and fills a table: body symmetry, body segmentation, body covering (skin, shell, exoskeleton, scales, feathers, hair), number and type of limbs, presence of a backbone, movement. They draw one labelled sketch. If available, a short video clip of animal phyla is used after observation, and groups can use textbook pages instead if there is no internet. Experts then return to home groups and each teaches their organisms' features using their table and drawing, while others add the information to a master table.
framework.teacherMoves: Set up stations before the lesson with specimens or labelled pictures. Remind about safety: 'Touch gently, wash hands, and return live animals to the garden.' Say: 'You are the expert. Your job is to find features that anyone, anywhere, could observe and check, not opinions like beautiful or useful.' Give 15 minutes for the expert groups. Circulate with questions: 'What do you see on the outside of its body? Does it have a backbone you can feel or see on the chart? How many legs, and are they jointed?' Prompt: 'Which feature would help us tell the snail from the earthworm?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. If a group is stuck, point to the textbook page on phyla features. Cold-call 2 experts per station to name one feature they will teach. In the home groups, give 4 minutes per expert and then announce 'Switch!'. Monitor that every learner speaks. Show the video (5 minutes) only if available; pause twice to ask 'Which feature just mentioned matches our specimens?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Jigsaw cooperative learning: each learner becomes responsible for one piece of the evidence, so all must communicate clearly and listen to peers (Communication and Collaboration). Using the same set of observable features for every animal supports the idea of a standard, shared system for classification.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each expert table has at least 4 completed feature columns for each specimen. (2) Labelled sketches show key features (e.g. segments of earthworm, shell of snail, 3 body parts and 6 jointed legs of insect, backbone of fish/lizard/goat). (3) In home groups, each learner teaches without reading word for word. (4) The master table is completed by all members. Use a checklist to record who can correctly say whether each animal has a backbone and an exoskeleton. Note misconceptions such as 'a worm and a snake are the same' or 'a butterfly is not an animal'.

framework.learnerExperience: Home groups use the master table to place each animal in a phylum: Annelida (earthworm), Mollusca (snail), Arthropoda (mosquito, butterfly), Chordata (chicken, lizard, goat, tilapia). They write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement for two animals of their choice, e.g. Claim: 'The earthworm belongs to Phylum Annelida.' Evidence: 'Its body is soft, long and divided into many similar rings (segments) and it has no legs or backbone.' Reasoning: 'Annelids are classified by having a segmented body, so the earthworm fits this phylum.' They also explain why the mosquito and the goat are in different phyla even though both can bite or feed on blood or grass. A Gallery Walk follows: groups display their re-sorted specimen cards with phylum labels and CER statements, and visitors leave a sticky note 'I agree because...' or 'I disagree because...' with a question. Groups compare their new scientific grouping with their Predict Phase groupings and discuss what changed.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You now have evidence. Scientists do not just say where an animal belongs, they defend it. Use the sentence frames: My claim is..., My evidence is..., This shows... because...' Model one CER on the board using the snail. Give 8 minutes for writing. Circulate and press: 'Is that feature observable? Could a learner in Mombasa check it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds for thinking. Start the Gallery Walk for 10 minutes with a rotation signal every 2 minutes. Ask visitors to give feedback respectfully (Respect). After the walk cold-call 5 learners: 'Which group's reasoning convinced you, and what evidence made you change your mind?' Then ask: 'Compare today's groups with your first groups. Which rules were not useful for everyone?' Highlight that body structure features give the same result no matter who uses them. Introduce terms phylum, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Chordata after learners have used the features, not before.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Gallery Walk: CER links each claim to observed features and to the classification principle, building scientific argumentation. The Gallery Walk exposes learners to other groups' reasoning and encourages respectful peer critique, which resolves the disagreement seen in the Predict Phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) CER statements name a phylum, cite at least two observed features and link them to the group characteristic. (2) Learners distinguish observable evidence from opinion. (3) Sticky-note feedback is specific and respectful. (4) Learners correctly explain why the earthworm (Annelida) differs from the snail (Mollusca) and why the mosquito and butterfly are both Arthropoda. Collect two CER statements per group for review; common errors (e.g. grouping by habitat) are revisited at the start of Lesson 6. Use a 3-question exit check: Which phylum has a backbone? Which has jointed legs and an exoskeleton? Which has segmented rings and no legs?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board: 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' In groups they write new questions or answers on sticky notes, e.g. 'If the goat and chicken are both Chordata, how are they different?', 'Why is a bat a mammal and not a bird?', 'How are insects different from spiders?', 'Are all Arthropoda harmful, like mosquitoes?'. They place notes under categories: Answered today, Partly answered, New questions. Learners move one earlier question to 'Answered' with evidence from today's table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look back at our board. Which of our questions can we answer with today's evidence? What new questions do the animals raise?' Give 3 minutes for silent writing, WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to read a question and place it on the board. Ask: 'Which question shows we need to look more closely within one phylum?' Highlight the question about how animals within the same phylum are classified. Link to the next lesson: 'All the Chordata we found share a backbone, yet a chicken, a lizard and a goat are very different. How do we tell them apart?' Praise questions that refer to the phenomenon organisms.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: it makes learners' growing understanding visible, connects each lesson to the anchoring phenomenon, and shows how evidence generates new questions that drive the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) At least one new question per group that refers to a specific organism. (2) Learners sort questions as answered or unanswered with a reason. (3) Some questions move beyond phylum level to classes within a phylum, showing readiness for Lesson 6. Note learners who still only ask naming questions (What is this called?) and encourage how/why questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups revise the class classification model started in earlier lessons. On chart paper they build or update a concept map/tree diagram with Kingdom Animalia at the top branching into the phyla Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Chordata, with the school organisms (earthworm, snail, mosquito, butterfly, chicken, lizard, goat) placed at the branches and the distinguishing feature written on each branch (e.g. 'segmented body, no legs', 'soft body with shell', 'jointed legs and exoskeleton', 'backbone'). They add Kingdom Plantae divisions from earlier lessons beside it and a note: 'Sorting rule must use observable features that everyone can check.' In a Think-Pair-Share, each learner finishes the sentences in the Summary Table prompt. Groups use a different colour to mark what changed from their first model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Return to our first model. What would you add, change or remove after today's evidence?' Provide chart paper and markers; allow 12 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'Which feature on this branch separates these animals from the others? Could a visitor from Nairobi use your model to identify the chicken?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one revision and the evidence that caused it. Remind learners to handle returned organisms carefully and release them in the garden (Animal Welfare). Close with: 'We can now say that animals are placed in phyla using body features. Next time we ask how animals within the same phylum are further classified.' Display models for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: updating a visible model with colour-coded changes helps learners see how evidence changes their thinking, linking the phenomenon of different groupings to a standard classification system based on shared features.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The model shows Kingdom Animalia branching to at least four phyla with distinguishing features. (2) All seven phenomenon animals are correctly placed. (3) Changes from the first model are marked and explained. (4) Learners can explain orally why a feature-based system works for everyone. Use the model and summary table as an exit ticket; learners who place organisms by habitat or use are given an extra pair of specimens to re-sort at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still used size, habitat or food use rather than body features, and what evidence showed the change in their thinking? Did every Jigsaw expert have enough specimens or pictures and textbook access, and what substitutes worked where live animals were missing? Which CER statements lacked observable evidence, and how will I address that early in Lesson 6? Did learners use Kiswahili or mother tongue productively before recording English scientific terms? Were safety and animal welfare rules followed, and were all organisms returned to the garden? Which new DQB questions show readiness to explore classes within Chordata and Arthropoda?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the earthworm has a soft segmented body with no legs, the snail has a soft body with a shell, the mosquito and butterfly have jointed legs and a hard outer covering (exoskeleton), and the chicken, lizard and goat all have a backbone but different body coverings (feathers, scales, hair).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that animals are classified into major phyla (Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Chordata) using observable body features such as segmentation, shell, jointed legs with an exoskeleton, and a backbone, not by size, colour, habitat or usefulness.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the school animals can be organised so anyone can identify them because phylum placement is based on shared, checkable body features. For example, the goat and the chicken are both Chordata because they both have a backbone, while the mosquito is Arthropoda because it has jointed legs and an exoskeleton. We still wonder how animals within the same phylum, such as the chicken, lizard and goat, are further classified.

LESSONS.title: Classes of Kingdom Animalia
LESSONS.aresKeywords: class, Chordata, Arthropoda, Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia, Insecta, Arachnida, Crustacea, Myriapoda, body covering, limbs, respiration, reproduction, dichotomous key

slo.purpose: Learners use observable features (body covering, limbs, respiration and reproduction) to divide animal phyla into classes, then defend their classifications with evidence. This advances the driving question 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' by showing that accurate classification needs finer, shared characteristics than size, colour or habitat.
slo.knowledge: b) classify organisms into phyla and classes of Kingdom Animalia. Phylum Chordata is divided into Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. Phylum Arthropoda is divided into Insecta, Arachnida, Crustacea and Myriapoda (Chilopoda and Diplopoda). Classes are separated by body covering, number and type of limbs, respiratory organs and mode of reproduction.
slo.skills: Observing and grouping animals using distinguishing characteristics; completing classification tables; constructing and using a simple dichotomous key; constructing explanations with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; arguing from evidence; communicating clearly to peers. Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration (speaking clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of specimens); Creativity and Imagination.
slo.attitudes: e) appreciate the diversity of plants and animals in nature. Values: Respect (considerate of others' opinions when groups disagree on classifications). Responsibility (cares for the environment and the animals handled). PCI: Animal Welfare (handles animals with care while observing and grouping them into Phylum Chordata and Arthropoda using distinguishing characteristics).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How are plants and animals classified?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1-5 learners met the problem that their own groupings (size, colour, habitat, usefulness as food) disagreed, and they learned about kingdoms, plant divisions and animal phyla. In Lesson 6 they see that phyla are still broad: a goat, chicken, lizard and the school's fish pictures are all Chordata, and a mosquito and butterfly are both Arthropoda, yet they differ. Classes are the next level. This raises the question for Lesson 7: 'How can we identify an unknown animal accurately?', which leads to dichotomous keys.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only locally available, harmless specimens (preserved or dead insects, snail shells, earthworms from the school garden, feathers, fish bones or pictures). Do not collect dangerous or unknown organisms (snakes, scorpions, wasps, bees, centipedes with bites). Do not handle live mosquitoes. Handle any live animal gently with a spoon or gloved hands, return it to where it was found, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards. Where specimens are unavailable, use drawings, photographs or textbook illustrations. Learners may discuss in Kiswahili or mother tongue, but record scientific terms in English.

LESSONS.overview: Anchoring phenomenon: the school collection (maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat) shows living things that cannot be grouped in one way that works for everyone. Today learners return to the animals in that collection. They predict how a goat, chicken and lizard might be grouped together, and how a mosquito and butterfly relate. Then, in a Jigsaw, expert groups examine specimens, pictures and charts for one class group (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals, and arthropod classes). They compare body covering, limbs, respiration and reproduction, and complete a classification table. Home groups then teach each other, test their ideas with a dichotomous-key challenge on the phenomenon animals, and defend a classification using CER. The lesson closes by updating the Driving Question Board and the class model of classification with the new idea that phyla are divided into classes using more specific characteristics. Materials: animal pictures/specimens, charts, classification cards, video (optional, offline copy if available), textbooks shared by groups, manila paper, markers.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the school collection from the phenomenon. Display or draw the animals: earthworm, snail, mosquito, butterfly, chicken, lizard and goat. Individually, each learner writes a prediction in their notebook: 'The chicken, lizard and goat are all in Phylum Chordata. Which features could we use to split them into smaller groups? Which feature would separate the mosquito from the butterfly, if any?' They draw a quick sketch grouping the 7 animals into smaller groups and give a reason for each group. Then Think-Pair-Share: pairs compare and note one place they disagree. Kiswahili may be used in discussion (e.g. 'ndege', 'mjusi', 'mamalia'), with scientific terms recorded in English.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the animals or the cards at the front. Say: 'Last lesson we placed animals in phyla. A goat, a chicken and a lizard are all Chordata. Are they the same? Think quietly and write your prediction first.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before anyone speaks. Allow 3 minutes for individual writing, then 3 minutes for pairs. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers): 'What feature did you use to split the chicken from the goat?' Record all predictions on the board without judging them as right or wrong. Ask: 'Whose grouping is different from your partner's? Why?' Circle features that appear repeatedly (skin covering, legs, wings, how it breathes, eggs or live young).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) combined with Think-Pair-Share. Making predictions first exposes learners' own grouping ideas (size, colour, habitat, usefulness as food) and creates a need for shared, observable characteristics. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner time to think and rehearse before speaking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 80% of learners write a prediction with a reason before talking; (2) number of pairs who name a structural feature (covering, limbs, breathing, reproduction) versus non-structural ones (size, colour, food use); (3) pairs who notice that their groupings differ and say so. Note misconceptions, such as 'all animals that fly are birds' (butterfly) or 'worms and snakes are the same' and revisit them in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Jigsaw, Part 1 (expert groups, 20 minutes). Class is divided into 6 expert groups of 5-6 learners. Each expert group receives a specimen/picture set, a chart and classification cards for ONE group: (1) Pisces (tilapia or omena from Lake Victoria, pictures of Nile perch); (2) Amphibia (frog/toad pictures); (3) Reptilia (lizard/agama pictures, tortoise, snake pictures only); (4) Aves (chicken feathers, egg, pictures of flamingo at Lake Nakuru); (5) Mammalia (goat or cow hair, skull/picture, pictures of a lion from Maasai Mara); (6) Arthropoda classes (dead mosquito and butterfly, spider picture, crab picture from Mombasa, millipede/centipede pictures). Groups examine the specimens carefully and complete a classification table with columns: body covering, limbs/appendages, respiration organs, reproduction (eggs or live young; external or internal fertilisation), and one other feature. Learners handle animals gently and return live animals (such as earthworms and snails) to the garden. If a video is available offline, groups may watch a short clip to check breathing and reproduction details; otherwise they use textbook pages. Jigsaw Part 2 (home groups, 15 minutes): learners regroup in mixed home groups with one expert from each class. Each expert teaches their class's features in 2 minutes while others fill in a master table.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and say: 'You are now the experts. Your task: find the features that make your group different from every other group. Look, touch gently, and record what you SEE, not what you guess.' Circulate with prompts: 'Show me where it breathes. What does its skin feel like? How many legs? Does it lay eggs or give birth?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each prompt. Prompt groups that are stuck: 'What does a mosquito have that a spider does not?' (antennae, 3 pairs of legs vs 4 pairs). For home groups, say: 'Teach, do not read. Each expert has 2 minutes. Others must ask one question.' Cold-call 3 home groups to share one feature that separates two classes. Stop at the 10-minute mark to check that tables are filling in. Remind learners about Animal Welfare: 'Be gentle. These are living things.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Jigsaw cooperative learning. Each learner becomes responsible for one piece of evidence, so everyone must contribute to the complete classification table. Comparing the same four characteristics across all classes helps learners see patterns (e.g. feathers only in birds, hair only in mammals, three body parts and six legs in insects) instead of memorising lists.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check expert tables for accuracy: correct covering (scales, moist skin, feathers, hair, exoskeleton), limbs, respiration (gills, lungs, skin, tracheae, book lungs) and reproduction. Observable indicators: learners point to the actual feature on the specimen when explaining; learners use class names correctly; every home group member speaks at least once. Look for the error 'frogs have scales' or 'insects have 8 legs' and correct it by asking learners to count or recheck.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their master table to build a claim about the animals in the phenomenon. Step 1 (Dichotomous-key challenge, 10 minutes): each home group writes a simple dichotomous key with 3-4 questions that separates the phenomenon animals (mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) into classes, using paired statements such as '1a. Has feathers - Aves; 1b. No feathers - go to 2'. Groups swap keys and test each other's keys with the classification cards. Step 2 (CER, 8 minutes): each learner writes a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning response to: 'Is a bat a bird or a mammal?' or 'Is a mosquito an insect or an arachnid?' Claim: the class of the animal. Evidence: at least two observed features from the tables. Reasoning: why those features define the class. Step 3: groups defend their classification when challenged by another group, and revise if the evidence supports a change. Learners link back: 'Why did our first groupings by size or colour disagree, and why do the class features not disagree?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your key must work for someone who has never seen these animals. Only use features you can observe.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the question 'Why can't we use colour in our key?' Before key swapping say: 'If the other group gets stuck, the problem is in the key, not the group.' During CER circulate and say: 'Show me the evidence in your table. Which feature proves your claim?' Cold-call 3 learners to read a CER aloud, then ask 2 other learners: 'Do you agree? What evidence would change your mind?' Introduce correct terms at this point (not before): Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia; Insecta, Arachnida, Crustacea, Myriapoda. Clarify tricky cases: a bat is a mammal (hair, milk, live young); a snail and earthworm are not arthropods or chordates (they belong to other phyla); a tilapia breathes with gills. Model the correct sentence frame: 'I claim that ___ belongs to class ___ because ___, which shows ___.' Use Kenyan examples (omena, tilapia, chameleon, ostrich, flamingo, goat, grasshopper, crab).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Dichotomous-key challenge plus Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER). Writing a key forces learners to choose clear, observable, either/or characteristics, which shows why scientists use shared features. CER trains learners to defend a classification with evidence and to revise their ideas when other groups present better evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 3-level CER check: Level 1 states a claim only; Level 2 gives a claim with a correct feature; Level 3 links two or more features to the class definition with reasoning. Aim for most learners at Level 2 or 3. Observe whether keys use observable paired statements and whether another group can use them to reach the correct class. Note which learners revise their ideas after challenge. Exit check: 'Name one feature that separates reptiles from amphibians.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board. Individually they write on sticky notes (a) one new thing they learned about classes of animals, and (b) one new question that has appeared (e.g. 'What if an animal has features of two classes?', 'How do we identify an animal we have never seen?', 'Where do viruses fit if they are not animals or plants?'). In groups they place the notes on the board under headings such as 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New questions'. The class discusses how this lesson answers part of 'How are plants and animals classified?' and leads to the next lesson question: 'How can we identify an unknown animal accurately?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board from Lesson 1. Which questions can we now answer? Take 30 seconds of silent thinking.' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to move a question from 'Unanswered' to 'Partly answered' or 'Answered' and justify it with evidence from today. Ask: 'What new question did the classes raise?' Highlight the question 'How can we identify an unknown animal accurately?' and say: 'In Lesson 7 we will use dichotomous keys more carefully to answer it.' Ensure that Respect is shown by thanking learners for questions that differ from yours.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board. Tracking questions and answers makes learning visible and shows learners how today's evidence connects to the unit driving question, keeping the lesson phenomenon-driven and learner-led.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sticky notes link to evidence from today (e.g. 'birds have feathers and lay eggs, so...'), that at least one new question per group goes beyond recall, and that learners can justify moving a question's status. Record which questions show lingering misconceptions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class classification model started in earlier lessons. On manila paper, each group updates a tree/flow diagram that began with the phenomenon animals: Kingdom Animalia, then phyla (Chordata, Arthropoda, others), and now classes with the key identifying features beneath each class (body covering, limbs, respiration, reproduction). They place the phenomenon animals (goat, chicken, lizard, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail) on the correct branches and mark with a different colour the ones that are not Chordata or Arthropoda. They add a short note: 'What this model explains' and 'What it cannot yet explain' (e.g. how to identify an unknown animal quickly). Groups then do a mini gallery walk (5 minutes), leaving one comment of agreement and one question on each other's models. Finally, learners complete the summary table prompt in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go back to our first puzzle: how can any person anywhere group these living things the same way? Show on your model how classes help.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after this question. Circulate and ask: 'Which feature put the lizard in Reptilia and not Amphibia?' Use the gallery walk: groups rotate every 90 seconds; instruct them 'Leave one star (agreement based on evidence) and one question.' Cold-call 3 groups to explain one change they made to their model from last lesson and the evidence that caused it. Close with: 'Phyla are broad groups. Classes use more specific characteristics. But a model is not complete until it helps us identify an animal we have never seen. That is tomorrow's question.' Collect models and tables for later assessment.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with a mini gallery walk. Revising a visible model shows how new evidence changes ideas, and peer feedback helps learners spot gaps and strengthen their explanations of how scientists organise living things.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: animals placed on correct class branches; at least two correct features per class; model revisions linked to evidence; gaps identified honestly (e.g. 'we cannot yet identify unknown animals'). Quick check: ask 3 learners to place the bat, the crab and the tilapia on the model and justify each. Use the summary table to confirm understanding.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson reflect: Did learners use observable features rather than size, colour or habitat when grouping? Which classes caused the most confusion (e.g. amphibians versus reptiles, insects versus arachnids)? Were all learners active in the Jigsaw, and did specimens or pictures provide enough evidence for each group? Which questions or WAIT TIME moments produced the deepest thinking? How well did the groups' CER responses connect features to class definitions? Did animals stay safe and were they returned to the environment? What adjustments are needed before Lesson 7, such as more practice with paired statements for dichotomous keys, additional local specimens (grasshopper, tilapia, chameleon) or additional use of Kiswahili for early discussion?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a goat, chicken, lizard and fish (all Chordata) differ in body covering (hair, feathers, scales), limbs, respiration (lungs, gills) and reproduction (eggs or live young), and that a mosquito, butterfly and crab (all Arthropoda) differ in number of legs, body parts and antennae.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that phyla can be divided further into classes using more specific characteristics: Chordata into Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia; Arthropoda into Insecta, Arachnida, Crustacea and Myriapoda.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the school animals can be organised into classes using shared, observable features (not size, colour or habitat), so anyone can classify them the same way, but we still need a reliable method to identify an unknown animal accurately, which leads to the next lesson.

LESSONS.title: Dichotomous keys for animals and viruses
LESSONS.aresKeywords: dichotomous key, couplet, observable features, Chordata, Arthropoda, virus, host cell, obligate parasite, biotechnology, vaccine, CER

slo.purpose: Learners construct and use a dichotomous key to identify the school-environment animals from the anchoring phenomenon (mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat), and brainstorm the general characteristics and economic importance of viruses, so they can revise their ideas about how to identify and classify living organisms accurately.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) outline the principles of constructing a dichotomous key (paired contrasting statements, observable features, one choice per step); (b) use a key to identify animals and place them in Phylum Chordata or Arthropoda; (c) state the general characteristics of viruses (non-cellular, only reproduce inside host cells, protein coat around DNA or RNA, no cell division or metabolism outside a host) and relate viruses to their economic importance in health, agriculture and biotechnology.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations and designing solutions (NGSS SEP 6): building a key. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): comparing group classifications. Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7): CER about a virus. Developing and using models (SEP 2): revising the classification model. Communication and Collaboration: speaks clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of various specimens.
slo.attitudes: Respect: considerate of others' opinions while brainstorming on the characteristics of viruses and their economic importance. Animal Welfare (PCI): handles animals with care while observing and grouping them into Phylum Chordata and Arthropoda. Appreciates the diversity of plants and animals in nature.
slo.keyInquiry: How are plants and animals classified? How are viruses important in nature? (Driving question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-6 showed that learner-made groupings by size, colour or usefulness differ between groups, and that shared structural features (plants, Chordata, Arthropoda) give a standard basis for grouping. Lesson 7 shows how a dichotomous key turns those features into a tool that lets anyone anywhere reach the same identification, and extends the system to viruses, which challenge the idea of a living organism. It sets up Lesson 8: How can our classification system help us explain biodiversity and the importance of viruses?
slo.safetyNotes: Use animal cards, photographs and preserved or already-dead specimens wherever possible. Do not collect dangerous or unknown organisms (snakes, scorpions, bees, wasps, unknown caterpillars). Handle any live earthworm, snail or insect gently, return it to where it was found, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards. Do not handle the mushroom or any unknown fungus. Do not touch sick or dead animals. Virus work uses diagrams only; no cultures are used.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the phenomenon: 'If all these organisms are living things, how can scientists organise them into groups so that any person anywhere can identify and study them?' They first predict how they would identify an unfamiliar animal from only a written description. Using animal cards (mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat, plus a Kenyan extra such as a tilapia from Lake Victoria and a grasshopper), groups build their own dichotomous key, swap keys with another group, and test whether a stranger reaches the same answer, which directly confronts the problem that subjective groupings (size, colour, usefulness) fail. They then compare their key with a prepared key and use it to place animals in Chordata or Arthropoda. In the second half, learners examine virus diagrams, readings and a short video (if available; a printed reading is the offline alternative) to build a list of virus characteristics and economic importance (maize lethal necrosis disease in Kenyan maize, cassava mosaic disease, HIV, measles and polio vaccines, COVID-19, and the use of viruses in biotechnology) and write a CER on whether a virus is a living organism. The Driving Question Board is updated and the class model of classification is revised to include keys and viruses.

framework.learnerExperience: Display the cards of a mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat, and ask: 'Imagine a visitor from Kisumu who has never seen your local organisms. You can only send them a written message. How can you make sure they name the same animal as you?' Learners individually write a prediction in their notebooks: (1) what kind of statements would work best in the message (e.g. 'it is big' versus 'it has six legs'), and (2) whether a virus can be placed in the same classification as the goat or the maize plant. They then think-pair-share and may use Kiswahili for the initial discussion. Scientific terms are recorded in English.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'In Lesson 1, groups made different groupings for the same organisms. Today we find out how to make a tool that gives the same answer for everyone.' Pose the question, then WAIT TIME of 12 seconds in silence before any talk. Give 2 minutes for individual writing, then 2 minutes for pairs. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'What kind of statement did you choose, and why?' Write phrases like 'big', 'beautiful', 'useful' and 'six legs', 'has a backbone' on the board in two columns without labelling them yet. Ask: 'Which column would two different people read the same way?' Do not tell the answer; record predictions for revisiting at the end of the lesson. Ask: 'Is a virus in the same group as the goat? Raise your hand for yes, no, not sure.' Record the count.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction in writing before instruction surfaces the idea that vague descriptions (big, beautiful) differ between people, and makes learners notice the conflict when their predictions are tested against evidence later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who write subjective features (size, colour, usefulness as food) versus those who write observable, countable features (number of legs, wings, backbone, shell); (2) the tally of yes/no/not sure on viruses as a baseline; (3) pairs who disagree and can say why. Note the names of 5 learners with subjective-only predictions for support during the construction task.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (about 30 minutes): Groups of 4 receive 8 animal cards (mosquito, butterfly, grasshopper, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, tilapia or goat) with photos and short observation notes (legs, wings, backbone, body segments, shell, body covering). Each group (1) lists observable differences, (2) builds a dichotomous key with paired contrasting statements, each leading to another couplet or an animal name, for example 'Backbone present / Backbone absent', then 'Feathers present / Scales or hair present', 'Six jointed legs / No jointed legs', (3) swaps keys with another group and tests it by identifying 3 'mystery' animals, and (4) records where the key failed or was ambiguous and fixes it. Groups then compare with a prepared key and sort the animals into Chordata or Arthropoda. If the school compound has safe specimens (e.g. a dead insect, a snail shell), learners may use them in addition. Part B (about 25 minutes): Learners use virus diagrams (e.g. bacteriophage, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus), textbook readings (groups share textbooks), and a short video if available, to build a table of virus characteristics (size, protein coat, genetic material, cannot reproduce outside a host cell) and a list of their importance: harmful (maize lethal necrosis disease and cassava mosaic disease in Kenyan farms, measles, polio, HIV, COVID-19, Newcastle disease in chicken, foot and mouth disease in cattle) and useful (vaccines, gene transfer in biotechnology, bacteriophages used against bacteria, biological control of pests). Learners should be considerate of others' opinions as they brainstorm.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Before starting say: 'A good key is like a path with forks. At every fork the visitor has only two choices, and both must be things anyone can see or count.' Model one couplet on the board with the earthworm and the snail. Prompt struggling groups with: 'Could two people disagree on this statement? If yes, change it.' When a group uses 'small / big', say: 'Small compared to what? Show me a feature that I can count.' Give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each question before offering hints. Set the timer: 10 minutes to build, 8 minutes to swap and test, 7 minutes to revise. Ask each group to nominate a tester who is not the author of the key. Remind learners to handle all specimens gently and return any live animals to where they were found (Animal Welfare). In Part B, hand out one virus diagram per group and ask: 'Where is the nucleus? Where are the mitochondria? What do you see instead?' Cold-call 5 groups to share one characteristic each and ask whether any group disagrees. Where internet is unavailable, use the printed virus reading and teacher-drawn diagram on the chalkboard. Ensure respectful turn-taking with the phrase: 'Build on the idea before you challenge it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Dichotomous-key challenge: converting shared, observable features into a fork-by-fork tool shows learners that classification works when statements are contrasting and objective, directly solving the problem from the phenomenon that subjective groupings differ between groups. Swapping keys is a built-in test of reliability. For viruses, comparing diagrams with cell structures builds understanding through contrast.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each couplet has two clearly contrasting statements using a countable or visible feature; (2) the swapped group reaches the intended animal for at least 3 of 3 mystery cards; (3) learners can correct a flawed couplet after testing; (4) animals are correctly placed in Chordata (chicken, lizard, goat, tilapia) or Arthropoda (mosquito, butterfly, grasshopper), with earthworm and snail correctly noted as neither; (5) in Part B, learners list at least 3 virus characteristics and 3 importance examples with at least one beneficial use. Record each group's tally of correct identifications on your checklist.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement for the question: 'Is a virus a living organism?' Claim: yes/no or 'it depends'. Evidence: at least two observations from the diagrams and reading (e.g. no cell structure, reproduces only inside a host cell, has genetic material). Reasoning: link to the characteristics of living things used in earlier lessons (nutrition, respiration, growth, reproduction, excretion, response, movement). They then think-pair-share, and 3 volunteers present to the class. Next, learners explain in pairs why the key they built works better than their earlier groupings by size, colour or usefulness, citing the evidence from their key test. Finally, they discuss in groups: 'How would a farmer in Trans Nzoia use a key and knowledge of viruses to protect a maize crop?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Make a claim you can defend with evidence from today. Opinions without evidence will not count.' Provide a CER frame on the board: 'I claim ... because ... which shows ... so ...'. WAIT TIME of 15 seconds after posing the CER question before writing begins. Give 5 minutes for writing, 3 for pairs. Cold-call 3 learners with different claims and ask the class: 'Who can add a piece of evidence or challenge the reasoning politely?' Probe: 'You said viruses are not alive. Which characteristic of living things does it fail, and which does it appear to show only inside a host?' Probe the key: 'Why did the swapped key give the same answer for everybody, when our earlier groupings did not?' Confirm the target idea: a key uses paired contrasting observable features; viruses are non-cellular and depend on a host cell, so they are not placed in the five kingdoms in the same way as organisms. Link to the economic examples: maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic, vaccines. Correct misconceptions: 'viruses are tiny bacteria' and 'antibiotics kill viruses'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Think-Pair-Share: requiring learners to link specific evidence to a general rule of what counts as living moves them from opinion to scientific argument, and public critique with respectful disagreement builds shared understanding. Returning to the Predict phase prediction helps learners see how their thinking has changed.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 3-point rubric: 1 = claim only; 2 = claim with one piece of evidence; 3 = claim, at least two pieces of evidence and reasoning linked to characteristics of living things. Aim for at least 70% of the class at level 2 or above; note learners at level 1 for follow-up. Listen for correct use of the terms couplet, host cell, protein coat, and for the ability to say why a key is more reliable than a subjective grouping. Collect 5 CERs as exit evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board. In their groups, they (1) place a sticky note answering part of the driving question ('How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?') with new evidence from today, such as 'A dichotomous key uses paired, observable contrasting features'; (2) mark earlier questions that are now answered (for example 'Why do our groupings differ?'); and (3) add at least one new question, such as 'How does classification help us explain how many different organisms live in Kenya?', 'Why do viruses keep changing (e.g. COVID-19 variants)?', or 'Can a key be made for plants from our school?'. Each group contributes at least one note.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we now answer with evidence? Which new ones does today raise?' Give 2 minutes of silent thinking, then WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before taking contributions. Cold-call 4 groups to read and place a note and explain the evidence behind it in one sentence. Move answered questions to an 'Answered' column with a coloured marker and ask: 'What was the evidence?' Push for questions that connect to the phenomenon: 'Which new question helps us explain why Kenya has so many different kinds of organisms and why viruses matter to farmers and health workers?' Highlight the question that leads to Lesson 8: 'How can our classification system help us explain biodiversity and the importance of viruses?' If the DQB is unavailable, use a chart paper or a chalkboard section.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: a visible, class-owned record of questions and answers connects each lesson's evidence to the unit's driving question and gives learners ownership of what to investigate next. Linking notes to evidence builds the habit of answering questions with data rather than recall.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes (1) cite evidence from today (a key test result or a virus characteristic); (2) show progress from earlier questions, such as moving from 'which grouping is best?' to 'which features are best for a key?'; (3) include at least one new question that is testable using the local environment or reading. Note groups that only copy facts from the textbook rather than posing questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class and individual models (a concept map or flow diagram started in Lesson 1 and revised in later lessons) of how living organisms are identified and classified. Each learner (1) adds a dichotomous key branch showing how to identify animals from the phenomenon collection (maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) at the level of Chordata and Arthropoda; (2) adds a box for viruses showing that they are non-cellular, need a host, and are important in health, agriculture and biotechnology; and (3) uses a different colour pen to mark what they changed since the Predict phase and why. They then revisit their opening prediction and write two sentences: 'I used to think ... Now I think ... because ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use a different colour to show what has changed in your thinking. Scientists keep track of how their ideas change.' Give 10 minutes of individual work, and circulate to ask 3 learners: 'What evidence made you add this part of your model?' WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each question. Then pair learners for 3 minutes to peer-review each other's models using the prompts: 'Is every link supported by evidence? Is anything missing?' Cold-call 3 learners to share one change. Revisit the Predict phase tally on whether viruses belong with the goat and ask learners to revise their vote with the evidence. Finish by posing the next question: 'Our system can name and group organisms. How might it help us explain the huge variety of life, and the importance of viruses, in Kenya?' Collect models for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: updating a visible model with a different colour makes the change in thinking explicit, and requiring evidence for each addition builds the habit of revising explanations in light of data. Peer review adds an external check on reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the model for: (1) a correct example of a dichotomous key linked to observable features; (2) viruses represented as non-cellular and host-dependent, with at least two examples of importance (one harmful, one beneficial); (3) a before/after statement that cites evidence from today; (4) linkages to the original phenomenon organisms. Use a quick 3-level rubric (missing / partial / complete) and record how many learners are at 'complete' to plan Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson reflect: (1) Did learners choose observable, countable features for the key, or did some stay with subjective ones like 'big' or 'beautiful'? Which prompts moved them? (2) Did the swap-and-test step reveal ambiguity in couplets, and did groups fix it without being told? (3) How did the class vote on whether a virus is alive change between Predict and Model Building? (4) Were any learners unable to take part because of limited textbooks or a lack of video access, and did the printed reading and chalkboard diagram work as alternatives? (5) Were animals handled with care and returned safely? (6) Which Kenyan examples (maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic disease, vaccines) engaged learners most, and what should be added in Lesson 8 on biodiversity? Note learners who need more support with writing couplets or CER before the next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? (Record how your dichotomous key worked when another group used it, which couplets were clear or confusing, which animals fell in Chordata and Arthropoda, and what the virus diagrams showed about structure.)
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? (A dichotomous key uses paired contrasting observable features to identify organisms reliably; viruses are non-cellular, have a protein coat and genetic material, and reproduce only inside host cells; viruses are important in health, agriculture and biotechnology.)
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help explain the phenomenon? (Explain why a key gives the same answer for everyone while groupings by size, colour or usefulness do not, and how knowing about viruses shows that classification must be based on shared observable characteristics. Raise a question for Lesson 8 on biodiversity.)

LESSONS.title: Synthesis and explanation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: classification, taxonomy, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Animalia, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta, Gymnospermae, Angiospermae, monocot, dicot, Chordata, Arthropoda, dichotomous key, viruses, biodiversity, claim, evidence, reasoning

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise evidence from Lessons 1-7 to explain how living organisms can be identified and classified accurately, and compare their final model with their Lesson 1 model.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: a) outline the general characteristics of organisms in Divisions Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta (including Gymnospermae and Angiospermae); b) classify organisms into phyla and classes of Kingdom Animalia (Chordata and Arthropoda); c) construct and use a dichotomous key to identify organisms; d) relate viruses to their economic importance in health, agriculture and biotechnology.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revising the classification model); Constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; Engaging in argument from evidence; Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information; Collaboration and communication when presenting keys.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the diversity of plants and animals in nature. Respect: be considerate of others' opinions while discussing and critiquing group models. Responsibility: care for the environment and the specimens used. Core competencies: Communication and Collaboration (speak clearly to peers while discussing distinguishing characteristics of specimens); Creativity and Imagination (experiment with varied ideas when designing keys and models). PCIs: Environmental Conservation (conserve biodiversity by collecting organisms responsibly); Animal Welfare (handle animals with care).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How are plants and animals classified? 2. How are viruses important in nature? Driving question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson. Learners return to the school-environment phenomenon (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) that first puzzled them because every group classified differently. They now use evidence from all lessons to show that a standard system based on shared observable characteristics lets anyone anywhere identify and study organisms. It closes the DQB and leads to the next question: How can classification knowledge be applied outside the classroom?
slo.safetyNotes: Use only familiar, safe, locally available specimens or cards/photographs; do not collect dangerous or unknown organisms (e.g. snakes, scorpions, unknown fungi). Wash hands after handling any specimen, soil or plants. Do not taste mushrooms or any specimen. Handle live animals gently and return them to where they were found (Animal Welfare). Collect no more plant material than needed and never uproot rare plants (Environmental Conservation). Keep walkways clear during the gallery walk.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the culminating synthesis lesson. Learners begin by predicting how they would now classify the original collection of organisms, then use a final classification challenge (organism cards/specimens plus a dichotomous key) as evidence of how far their thinking has moved. In the Explain phase they write and defend a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Final Explanation answering the driving question 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' The class then completes the Driving Question Board, marking which questions are answered and which new ones remain, and finally compares their Lesson 1 model with the final model. The lesson ends with the new question: How can classification knowledge be applied outside the classroom? Learners may discuss in Kiswahili or mother tongue, but scientific terms are recorded in English. The lesson does not depend on internet; the video is optional and can be replaced by charts and learners' notes.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners view the display of organisms from the school environment (maize plant, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) as real specimens, photographs or cards. In pairs they individually write a prediction: 'Mixed in with a new set of 6 unfamiliar organisms from Kericho, Kisumu or Mombasa, could a learner from another school classify them exactly as we do? What would we need so that the answer is yes?' They then share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share), discussing first in Kiswahili or mother tongue if helpful, and record key terms in English.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the organisms and say: 'In Lesson 1 we asked: if all these are living things, how can scientists organise them so anyone, anywhere, can identify them? Today you will answer that with evidence.' Pose the prediction question and give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking, then 2 minutes to write. Pair learners for 3 minutes. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'What would another learner in Kisumu need to get the same groups as you?' Listen for 'same characteristics', 'a key', 'standard names'. Record answers on the board without evaluating. Say: 'Let us test these predictions today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) reprise with Think-Pair-Share: Writing predictions before the challenge makes learners commit to ideas drawn from earlier lessons, so they can later see how evidence confirms or changes their thinking. Pairing lets learners rehearse scientific vocabulary before whole-class talk.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of predictions mention a shared, observable characteristic or a key (not size, colour or usefulness as food). Indicators: learners use terms like 'dichotomous key', 'division', 'phylum', 'class'; note learners who still propose arbitrary groupings for follow-up. Tally the ideas on the board for comparison at the end.

framework.learnerExperience: Final classification challenge (groups of 4). Each group receives organism cards/specimens (maize, bean, fern, moss, pine/cypress leaf or cone from Kenyan highlands, mushroom picture, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat, plus 2 new unfamiliar cards, e.g. a sisal plant and a tilapia from Lake Victoria). Task 1: sort them into Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia and then into Divisions (Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta; Gymnospermae/Angiospermae; monocot/dicot) and Phyla/Classes (Chordata: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals; Arthropoda: insects, arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods). Task 2: build or complete a dichotomous key for at least 6 organisms and exchange it with another group, who must use it to identify an unlabelled 'mystery' organism. Task 3: record where the key was unclear. Groups present their models/keys in a short gallery-style rotation (2 minutes per station), with learners recording evidence in their notes and tick-checking the rubric. Groups also add a one-line note on viruses: why they are not placed in either kingdom, and their importance (e.g. vaccines, maize streak virus in crops, biotechnology). Optional 5-minute video or chart review to confirm characteristics.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your challenge is to classify the same organisms as before, but this time using shared, observable characteristics.' Distribute cards and rubrics. Circulate and ask: 'Which characteristic did you use for that split? Could a learner in Mombasa observe it too?' and 'Where does the mushroom fit, and why does it not fit Plantae?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call at least 6 learners across groups, including quieter learners. Prompt for Animal Welfare: 'How are we handling the live earthworm or snail?' Remind groups to use only safe specimens and to return live ones to the school garden. During key exchange say: 'The test of a good key is whether a stranger can use it. Note exactly where they got stuck.' Move through the stations asking each group to justify one choice. For viruses ask: 'Give one harm and one benefit of viruses to Kenyans.' Listen for maize streak virus, HIV/measles/COVID-19, vaccines, gene therapy and biotechnology.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Dichotomous-key challenge with gallery presentations: Using and testing another group's key shows that accurate identification depends on clear, observable, yes/no characteristics, directly addressing the Lesson 1 problem where each group's classification differed. Gallery presentation exposes learners to multiple models so they can compare evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) groups correctly place at least 10 of 13 organisms into the right division, phylum or class; (2) keys use observable paired statements (e.g. 'has wings / no wings', 'seeds in fruit / seeds not in fruit', 'one cotyledon / two cotyledons', 'vertebral column present / absent'); (3) the exchanging group identifies the mystery organism correctly; (4) learners can name one importance of arthropods (pollination, pests, disease vectors such as mosquitoes) and one of viruses. Record on a checklist and note misconceptions, e.g. 'mushroom is a plant' or 'viruses are cells'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write an individual Final Explanation answering the driving question using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER). Claim: a statement answering 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' Evidence: at least three pieces from the lessons and the challenge (e.g. moss lacks vascular tissue while fern has vascular tissue and spores; maize has parallel veins and one cotyledon whereas bean has net veins and two cotyledons; mosquito has 3 pairs of legs and a jointed exoskeleton so is in Arthropoda, while chicken has a backbone so is in Chordata; a key gave the same answer for two different groups). Reasoning: explains why shared, observable characteristics and standard names produce the same grouping for any learner, unlike groupings by size, colour or food use. They also include one sentence on the importance of viruses. Then they do Think-Pair-Share to critique a partner's CER using the rubric and revise.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the CER frame: 'I claim that ... The evidence is ... This shows that ... because ...'. Say: 'Your claim must answer the driving question, and your evidence must come from what we observed, not from memory only.' Give 8 minutes of silent writing. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds when asking: 'Why did our groups disagree in Lesson 1 but agree today?' Cold-call 3 learners to share claims and 3 to share the strongest evidence. Probe: 'Is size or colour good evidence for classification? Why not?' and 'How does a dichotomous key help someone who has never seen this organism?' Press for reasoning that links characteristics to a standard system. Use the rubric to give feedback: 'Your evidence is clear; now explain why it supports your claim.' Allow Kiswahili for discussion but require written English terms.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Think-Pair-Share: CER requires learners to connect specific evidence to a general principle, building a scientifically defensible explanation. Peer critique strengthens argumentation and clarifies gaps in reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-level rubric: (1) Claim answers the driving question; (2) at least 3 accurate pieces of evidence from Plantae, Animalia and the key activity; (3) reasoning links evidence to the need for shared observable characteristics and a standard system; (4) correct scientific terms (division, phylum, class, dichotomous key). Look for revised wording after peer feedback. Learners who give only a list of organisms without reasoning get a follow-up prompt: 'What makes this feature a reliable way to group them?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB built since Lesson 1. In groups they sort the question cards into 'Answered with evidence', 'Partly answered' and 'Not yet answered'. For each answered question they attach a sticky note with the evidence and the lesson where it was found (for example, 'Why do groups classify differently?' answered by Lessons 1 and 4; 'How are viruses important?' answered in Lesson 7). They then write at least one new question that goes beyond the classroom, such as: 'How can classification knowledge be applied outside the classroom, for example in farming, health and conservation in Kenya?' and add it to the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'Let us see how far our questions have travelled.' Give each group 5 minutes to sort cards. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking: 'Which question can we now answer with confidence, and what is your evidence?' Cold-call 4 groups to present one answered question each, and 2 groups to share a question still open. Ask: 'Which unanswered question could farmers in Kericho or conservationists at Lake Naivasha help us with?' Guide learners to the new question. Celebrate respect by thanking learners who built on a peer's idea. Do not discard unanswered questions; mark them for future study.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: Revisiting the DQB makes learning progress visible, shows that learner questions drove the unit, and links the final explanation to the original phenomenon while generating a new inquiry for the next topic.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups can match at least 80% of the answered questions to specific evidence and lesson numbers. Indicators: learners cite activities (the key exchange, monocot/dicot comparison, arthropod classes) rather than say 'the teacher said'. Check that new questions are testable and relate to application, e.g. 'How can a key help identify crop pests in Nakuru?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their Lesson 1 models (their first grouping of the organisms) and draw or build a final model, such as a classification tree/flow chart showing Kingdom Plantae and Animalia, divisions of Plantae, phyla and classes of Animalia, a short note on viruses as non-cellular, and a small dichotomous key. In pairs they compare Lesson 1 and final models using a 'Then and Now' table: What we grouped by; Why it changed; Evidence; What is still uncertain. Several learners share how their thinking changed. Finally they complete the Summary Table (What we observed / What we learned / How we can explain it).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your first model. Now draw your best model that would let any learner in Kenya reach the same groups.' Give 10 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'What did you add or change, and what evidence made you change it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to describe one specific change, e.g. from grouping by 'things we eat' to grouping by 'presence of seeds'. Ask: 'Can your model place a new organism you have never seen, say a tilapia or a cypress tree?' Close by returning to the phenomenon: 'We began puzzled that our groups differed. What have we figured out?' Introduce the next question: 'How can classification knowledge be applied outside the classroom?' Set a homework thought: find one place in your home or community (farm, clinic, market in Kisumu) where classification or identification keys are used.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: Comparing the Lesson 1 model with the final model makes conceptual change explicit, helping learners see that science improves ideas using evidence. It also consolidates that standard classification solves the original phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators of a strong final model: (1) uses shared observable characteristics rather than size, colour or use; (2) shows hierarchy from kingdom to division/phylum to class; (3) includes a functioning dichotomous key; (4) places viruses appropriately and notes their importance; (5) the 'Then and Now' table cites evidence for at least 3 changes. Learners who still use subjective groupings receive a one-to-one prompt using a specimen card.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners moved from grouping by size, colour or food use to grouping by shared observable characteristics, and what evidence in their CER or model shows it? Did the key exchange expose specific weak points (e.g. confusion between monocot and dicot features, or insect and arachnid features)? Which DQB questions remain unanswered, and how will they be used in the next lesson on applying classification outside the classroom? Were Kiswahili and mother tongue discussions supporting understanding, and did all learners record English terms? Were safety and animal welfare rules followed? What would you change about specimens or time allocation next time?

When we used shared, observable characteristics and dichotomous keys, different groups reached the same results.

We learned how to build and use dichotomous keys and that viruses are non-cellular but important in health, agriculture and biotechnology.
