FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Biology Grade 11 – Sub-strand 1.3 Taxonomy II: Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Driving question: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately? You will write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Final Explanation using what you observed in Lessons 1 to 8 about the organisms around our school: maize, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard and goat. Answer each section in the space below it. Use evidence from your own observations, your group work and your Driving Question Board. Use your own words and record scientific terms in English. You may discuss ideas in Kiswahili or your mother tongue before you write. Then use your answers to help your group build its Local Biodiversity Classification Guide.

sections.title: Part 1: The problem with our own groupings
sections.prompt: In Lesson 1 your group sorted the organisms from around the school and compared your grouping with other groups in a gallery walk. (a) What rules did different groups use, and what did you notice when you compared the groupings? (b) Explain why a standard system of classification is needed so that any person anywhere can identify and study an organism.
sections.exemplar: (a) Different groups sorted the organisms by size, colour, habitat or usefulness as food. When we compared the groupings in the gallery walk they did not agree, because every group chose different rules, so no single grouping worked for everyone. (b) A standard system is needed because personal rules give different results for different people. If everyone uses the same shared, observable characteristics, any person anywhere can identify and study an organism and get the same result. This lets scientists organise and communicate about living things accurately.

sections.title: Part 2: Classifying plants
sections.prompt: Use the plants you examined (moss, fern, maize and bean plants). (a) Name the three plant groups you studied and state the observable features that place a plant in each group. (b) Explain why grouping plants by these features is more reliable than grouping them by size, colour or use as food.
sections.exemplar: (a) Bryophyta (moss): small, rhizoids instead of true roots, no vascular tissue, spores in capsules, grows in damp places. Pteridophyta (fern): true roots, a rhizome, fronds with brown sori on the underside, vascular tissue, reproduces by spores, no seeds or flowers. Spermatophyta (maize and bean): roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue, reproduce by seeds; maize and beans produce flowers and seeds (grains and pods), and can be divided into monocots and dicots. (b) These features can be observed and checked by anyone, so every group places a plant in the same division. Size, colour or use as food depend on personal opinion, so groups disagreed, and moss, for example, was wrongly placed with grass or 'small green things'.

sections.title: Part 3: Classifying animals
sections.prompt: Think about the animals in our collection (earthworm, snail, mosquito, butterfly, chicken, lizard, goat). (a) Choose three animals from different phyla and write a CER statement placing each in its phylum, using observable body features. (b) Explain how the goat, chicken and lizard are further separated within their phylum.
sections.exemplar: (a) Claim: the earthworm is in Annelida, the snail is in Mollusca and the mosquito is in Arthropoda. Evidence: the earthworm has a soft segmented body with no legs; the snail has a soft body with a shell; the mosquito has jointed legs and a hard outer covering (exoskeleton). Reasoning: phyla are decided by shared, checkable body features such as segmentation, a shell, jointed legs with an exoskeleton, or a backbone, not by size, colour or habitat, so anyone examining the animal reaches the same phylum. (b) The goat, chicken and lizard are all Chordata because they have a backbone. Phyla are divided into classes using more specific features such as body covering, limbs, respiration and reproduction: the goat has hair (Mammalia), the chicken has feathers (Aves) and the lizard has scales (Reptilia). Arthropoda are likewise divided into classes, for example Insecta, where the mosquito and butterfly belong.

sections.title: Part 4: Dichotomous keys
sections.prompt: (a) Describe how a dichotomous key is built and used. (b) Write the first two couplets of a key you could use to separate three organisms from our collection. (c) Explain why different groups using the same key reach the same answer, unlike your Lesson 1 groupings.
sections.exemplar: (a) A dichotomous key is a set of numbered couplets. Each couplet gives two contrasting, observable choices; you choose the one that fits the organism and follow it to the next couplet until you reach one name. (b) Example for moss, fern and maize: 1a. Plant has no true roots or vascular tissue: moss (Bryophyta). 1b. Plant has true roots and vascular tissue: go to 2. 2a. Reproduces by spores on the underside of fronds, no seeds: fern (Pteridophyta). 2b. Reproduces by seeds: maize (Spermatophyta). (c) The key uses clear, observable features, not personal opinions such as size, colour or usefulness. Each step has only two choices, so different people following the same couplets get the same identification, whereas our own groupings depended on the rules each group invented.

sections.title: Part 5: Viruses and the final explanation
sections.prompt: (a) What are the characteristics of viruses, and give two examples of why they are important in agriculture, health or biotechnology. (b) Now write your Final Explanation for the driving question 'How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?' Use a claim, evidence from at least two lessons, and reasoning. Say how your thinking has changed since your Lesson 1 model.
sections.exemplar: (a) Viruses are non-cellular, have a protein coat and genetic material, and reproduce only inside host cells, so they differ from cellular organisms. They matter in agriculture because maize lethal necrosis disease harms Kenyan maize and cassava mosaic disease harms cassava; in health because viruses cause HIV, measles, polio and COVID-19, and vaccines protect against some of them; and viruses are also used in biotechnology. (b) Claim: Living organisms can be identified and classified accurately by using a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics, together with tools such as dichotomous keys. Evidence: In Lesson 1 our groupings of the school organisms by size, colour or usefulness differed from group to group. Later we placed plants into Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta using features like rhizoids, sori on fern fronds and seeds, and placed animals into phyla such as Chordata and Arthropoda and then into classes using features like backbone, jointed legs, and hair, feathers or scales. When different groups used dichotomous keys they reached the same answer. Reasoning: Because these features can be checked by anyone, the same organism is placed in the same group by everyone, so anyone anywhere can study and communicate about biodiversity. This replaces our Lesson 1 groupings, which varied between groups. Viruses show that classification depends on structure and characteristics, since they are non-cellular. A remaining question is how classification knowledge can be applied outside the classroom.

rubric.excellent: Gives a clear claim that a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics and dichotomous keys allows accurate identification and classification.
rubric.proficient: Gives a claim about classification but it is general or only partly linked to observable characteristics and keys.
rubric.developing: Claim is missing, unclear or does not answer the driving question.

rubric.excellent: Uses specific evidence from several lessons, such as the school organisms, moss, fern, maize, bean, earthworm, snail, mosquito, goat, chicken and lizard, and the key results.
rubric.proficient: Uses some correct evidence from the lessons but it is limited or lacks detail.
rubric.developing: Evidence is vague, incorrect or not taken from the lessons.

rubric.criterion: Scientific reasoning and use of terms
rubric.excellent: Explains why observable shared features give the same result for everyone while size, colour or use do not, and uses divisions, phyla, classes, couplets and viruses correctly.
rubric.proficient: Gives some reasoning and uses most terms correctly.
rubric.developing: Little or no reasoning; terms are missing or misused.

rubric.excellent: Writes correct contrasting couplets and accurately describes virus characteristics and their importance with Kenyan examples.
rubric.proficient: Writes a mostly workable key and gives some correct virus facts.
rubric.developing: Key is not workable and virus ideas are missing or incorrect.

rubric.excellent: Clearly compares the Lesson 1 groupings with the final model and states a relevant new question.
rubric.proficient: Mentions that thinking changed but with limited comparison.
rubric.developing: Does not show how thinking has changed.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we identify and classify living organisms accurately?

lessons.title: Why classify organisms?
lessons.observed: We observed 13 local organisms (maize, bean plant, grass, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) and noted that they differ in structure, size, body covering, movement and reproduction. Different groups sorted them in different ways (by size, colour, habitat, usefulness).
lessons.learned: Organisms can be grouped using similarities and differences, but groupings made with different rules do not agree. Scientists need a standard system of classification based on shared, observable characteristics.
lessons.explained: Because everyone chose different rules, no single grouping worked for everyone. A standard system uses the same observable characteristics so that any person anywhere can identify and study an organism and get the same result. We still need to find out how scientists decide which characteristics to use.

lessons.title: Kingdom Plantae — Bryophyta
lessons.observed: Describe what you observed in the moss with a hand lens: its size, the base (rhizoids), the stem-like and leaf-like parts, any spore capsules, where it was growing, and how it differed from maize or bean plants.
lessons.learned: State the characteristics that identify Division Bryophyta (e.g. small size, rhizoids instead of true roots, no vascular tissue, spores in capsules, damp habitats) and how they differ from other plants.
lessons.explained: Explain why moss stays small and grows in damp places, and how this evidence helps scientists classify plants more accurately than grouping by size, colour or use. What new question do you now have about how other plants differ from bryophytes?

lessons.title: Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
lessons.observed: We observed that ferns have true roots, a rhizome and fronds with brown sori on the underside, while maize and bean plants have roots, stems, leaves and flowers that produce seeds (grains and pods). Moss has no true roots and no vascular tissue.
lessons.learned: Pteridophytes reproduce by spores and have vascular tissue but no seeds or flowers; spermatophytes reproduce by seeds and have vascular tissue; bryophytes lack vascular tissue and true roots. These are shared, observable features anyone can check.
lessons.explained: These features help explain our phenomenon because they give everyone the same rules for grouping plants, instead of personal groupings by size, colour or use as food. We still need a step-by-step way to identify an unknown plant.

lessons.title: Using Dichotomous Keys
lessons.observed: We used a sample dichotomous key and a ruler to identify local plants (maize, bean, grass, fern, moss, sukuma wiki) and found that different group members reached the same name when they followed the same couplets.
lessons.learned: A dichotomous key uses pairs of contrasting, observable characteristics, in numbered couplets, so that each step has only two choices and leads to one identification. Features such as true roots, stems and leaves, fronds, seeds, and parallel versus net veins help place plants into Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta (monocots and dicots).
lessons.explained: A key gives the same answer to everyone because it uses clear, observable features rather than personal opinions such as size, colour or usefulness. This is how scientists can organise the organisms around our school so that anyone can identify them. New question: can the same method be used to identify animals?

lessons.title: Kingdom Animalia — major phyla
lessons.observed: We observed that the earthworm has a soft segmented body with no legs, the snail has a soft body with a shell, the mosquito and butterfly have jointed legs and a hard outer covering (exoskeleton), and the chicken, lizard and goat all have a backbone but different body coverings (feathers, scales, hair).
lessons.learned: We learned that animals are classified into major phyla (Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Chordata) using observable body features such as segmentation, shell, jointed legs with an exoskeleton, and a backbone, not by size, colour, habitat or usefulness.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the school animals can be organised so anyone can identify them because phylum placement is based on shared, checkable body features. For example, the goat and the chicken are both Chordata because they both have a backbone, while the mosquito is Arthropoda because it has jointed legs and an exoskeleton. We still wonder how animals within the same phylum, such as the chicken, lizard and goat, are further classified.

lessons.title: Classes of Kingdom Animalia
lessons.observed: We observed that a goat, chicken, lizard and fish (all Chordata) differ in body covering (hair, feathers, scales), limbs, respiration (lungs, gills) and reproduction (eggs or live young), and that a mosquito, butterfly and crab (all Arthropoda) differ in number of legs, body parts and antennae.
lessons.learned: We learned that phyla can be divided further into classes using more specific characteristics: Chordata into Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia; Arthropoda into Insecta, Arachnida, Crustacea and Myriapoda.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the school animals can be organised into classes using shared, observable features (not size, colour or habitat), so anyone can classify them the same way, but we still need a reliable method to identify an unknown animal accurately, which leads to the next lesson.

lessons.title: Dichotomous keys for animals and viruses
lessons.observed: What did we observe? (Record how your dichotomous key worked when another group used it, which couplets were clear or confusing, which animals fell in Chordata and Arthropoda, and what the virus diagrams showed about structure.)
lessons.learned: What did we learn? (A dichotomous key uses paired contrasting observable features to identify organisms reliably; viruses are non-cellular, have a protein coat and genetic material, and reproduce only inside host cells; viruses are important in health, agriculture and biotechnology.)
lessons.explained: How does this help explain the phenomenon? (Explain why a key gives the same answer for everyone while groupings by size, colour or usefulness do not, and how knowing about viruses shows that classification must be based on shared observable characteristics. Raise a question for Lesson 8 on biodiversity.)

lessons.title: Synthesis and explanation
lessons.observed: We observed that organisms from our school environment (maize, bean, fern, moss, mushroom, mosquito, butterfly, earthworm, snail, chicken, lizard, goat) differ in structure, body covering, movement and reproduction, and that groups using size, colour or usefulness produced different groupings. When we used shared, observable characteristics and dichotomous keys, different groups reached the same results.
lessons.learned: We learned that plants are classified into Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta (Gymnospermae and Angiospermae; monocots and dicots), and animals into phyla such as Chordata and Arthropoda and then classes. We learned how to build and use dichotomous keys and that viruses are non-cellular but important in health, agriculture and biotechnology.
lessons.explained: We can explain that organisms can be identified and classified accurately by using a standard system based on shared, observable characteristics and tools such as dichotomous keys, so that anyone anywhere can study and communicate about biodiversity. This replaces our Lesson 1 groupings, which varied from group to group.
